Last night, after I came out of the restaurant, I discovered my phone was gone.
Actually I didn't even know when the phone fell out, because I hadn't used it the whole time.
I searched through everything in my bag once, but I still couldn't find it.
Although I was very anxious, my friend comforted me, saying: "Don't worry, we can use the map function to find the phone's location."
According to the location on the map, we went back to the restaurant entrance and found the phone was right under a chair.
The waitress said that when she was cleaning up just now, she hadn't noticed it either.
After finding the phone, I was so happy that I almost cried.
From then on, I developed a good habit: before going out, I always make sure to check whether I've brought everything.
Yesterday was the Mid-Autumn Festival, and my Chinese friend invited me to his home for dinner.
After dinner, we sat outside, eating mooncakes while watching the moon.
My friend's grandma said, "In the whole year, the Mid-Autumn moon is the roundest."
She also told us an old story about the moon; it was really interesting.
The mooncakes were a little sweet; I ate two pieces and also drank a cup of hot tea.
My friend told me that at Mid-Autumn Festival, the family should be together — this is called "tuanyuan", reunion.
Looking at the big, round moon, I started to miss home too, so I gave my mom a call.
Mom said with a smile, "Although you are far from home, the moon we see is the same one."
Last week we moved, because the old place was too far from my office.
Although the new home isn't big, it's both clean and quiet.
On moving day, a few friends came to help us carry boxes, and everyone was worn out.
At noon we didn't have a table yet, so we just sat on the floor and ate noodles.
In the evening, the neighbors brought over some fruit and said, "Welcome!"
The new home is very close to the subway station — a five-minute walk and you're there.
Now I like this new home more and more.
In the evening, my friend and I went to a restaurant together and ordered a lot of dishes.
After we finished eating, we called the waiter over to pay the bill.
My friend wanted to pay, and I wanted to pay too — we both wanted to treat.
The waiter had just said how much it was when I jumped in: "This one's on me!"
My friend also wanted to pay and said: "No way — today it should be me treating."
I grabbed the money, ran over to the waiter, and handed it to her first.
Once we were outside the restaurant, my friend said: "Then let me buy you a cup of coffee!"
Half a year ago, I moved to a new place.
Back then I didn't know anyone; every day after work I came home to a very quiet house.
My neighbor is an auntie in her sixties who exercises by the entrance every morning.
One day she brought me a bowl of hot noodles and said: "Even living alone, you should still eat properly."
On weekends, I help her carry heavy things upstairs.
Now we often drink tea and chat together.
When my mom asked whether I was used to living alone, I said: "Don't worry — I have a neighbor who is just like family."
Today at noon, my colleague and I went to a restaurant together for lunch.
The waiter brought the menu and asked what dishes we wanted to eat.
My colleague loves spicy food, and he ordered an especially spicy dish.
I said, "I don't eat spicy food — you two order, I'll get something of my own."
I asked the waiter: "Is this dish spicy?" The waiter said: "Not spicy — don't worry."
After the food arrived, my colleague drank water the whole time while eating.
My dish wasn't spicy at all — it was delicious, and I finished it all by myself.
Saturday evening, it suddenly started raining outside, and I was at home watching TV.
My neighbor forgot her umbrella and stood at the door, asking me: "Can I borrow an umbrella?"
I said: "Of course you can, just wait a moment."
I fetched her an umbrella, she said thanks, and left.
The next day, the weather was nice, and my neighbor returned the umbrella and also brought some fruit.
I said: "You're so kind, thank you."
At noon we ate the fruit together and chatted too.
Last week, I bought a coat online.
The color in the photo looked great, but after the coat arrived, the color was completely different from the photo.
Moreover, the size was also a little small, and it felt very uncomfortable once I put it on.
So I decided to apply for a return, and sent a message to customer service.
Customer service replied very quickly, telling me to wrap the coat up again and mail it back.
Although mailing the courier took a little time, the whole process wasn't troublesome at all.
Three days later, the money was refunded to my account.
This experience taught me that before buying clothes online, it's best to look at the size chart clearly first.
I just came to Beijing for work, and this morning I went to the bank to open an account.
There were a lot of people in the bank; after taking a number, I sat waiting for half an hour.
The staff member asked me: "Did you bring your passport?"
I said: "Yes, here are my passport and my phone number."
She had me write my name and also asked me to think of a password.
Fifteen minutes later, I got my new bank card.
With a bank card, I can now spend money with my phone to buy things — so convenient!
In the evening I didn't feel like cooking, so I used my phone to order delivery.
I ordered a dish and a bowl of rice, twenty kuai in total.
The delivery person called me and said: "I'm downstairs."
I hurried downstairs, took the delivery, and said thanks to him.
Back home, the food was still hot — the dish was delicious, and the rice was good too.
Ordering delivery like this is much faster than cooking myself.
My mom, though, says delivery is never as good as what you cook at home.
Last month my phone suddenly broke, and I needed to buy a new one right away.
But I didn't have that much money, so I borrowed a thousand yuan from my colleague Xiao Wang.
Xiao Wang said with a smile: "No problem — pay me back whenever you have the money."
Yesterday I finally got this month's salary.
The first thing I did was go find Xiao Wang to pay him back.
I gave the thousand yuan back to him and also treated him to a cup of coffee.
Xiao Wang said happily: "Thanks — you really are a good friend!"
I think borrowing money is easy, but you should be even quicker about paying it back — only then will a friendship get better and better.
My friend and I went to the store to buy things; we bought a lot, and had to pay more than three hundred yuan.
I looked at my money and realized it wasn't enough.
I asked the clerk: "Can I pay by card?"
The clerk said: "You can't pay by card here — you can pay with your phone."
I said: "Okay, then I'll pay with my phone."
I paid with my phone, and it was done very quickly.
My friend said: "Next time you're short on money, I'll help you pay."
Summer is almost here, and my wife and I are planning to take a trip.
I want to visit a city in the south, but my wife would rather go mountain climbing.
In the end we decided to first spend three days in the southern city, and then go mountain climbing.
I looked at many photos online; the city is clean and beautiful, with trees all along the streets.
My wife said: "We should buy the plane tickets early — more and more people are flying these days."
After buying the tickets, I put the map and the camera into the suitcase.
If it rains on the day of the climb, we'll just spend one more day in the city.
In just two weeks we'll be off on our trip, and my wife and I are both really excited.
This morning, the teacher gave us the results of this exam.
I looked at my phone while nervously waiting.
The moment I saw the score, I was extremely happy.
My grade was even better than I expected, and my mom was very happy too when she found out.
A classmate asked me: "How did you do so well on the exam?"
I said with a smile: "Because I review seriously every day."
This grade made me very happy, and I want to keep working hard.
My home isn't too far from my company, but I take the bus to work every day, and it's always crowded.
Last month a colleague said to me: "Why don't you ride a bike to work? It's convenient and it's good exercise."
I thought he was right, so I bought a new bicycle.
The first day I rode, my legs were sore and I rode very slowly.
But I rode every day, and after a week I was riding faster and faster.
Every morning I look at the trees and flowers along the street while I ride, and it feels wonderful.
Now I'm used to biking to work, and my health is much better than before.
Riding a bike is also good for the environment, and I plan to keep riding from now on.
Last month I noticed that we were using a lot more water at home than before.
I had a look around, and only then did I find that the bathroom tap had not been turned off properly.
I turned it off right away, and from that day on I began to pay attention to how we use water.
These days my showers are shorter than they used to be, and when I brush my teeth I always turn the tap off.
The water left over from washing clothes I use to clean the room, so nothing at all is wasted.
My neighbour, an older lady, told me that the place where she grew up often had no water, so she is extremely careful with it.
She said: "Water looks cheap, but it is actually extremely important."
One person alone does not save much water, but if everyone did this, the world would be a different place.
Next week I'm going on a business trip, and there'll be no one at home to water the flowers.
I went downstairs to find my neighbor Xiao Zhang and said: "Xiao Zhang, sorry to trouble you, could you water the flowers for me?"
Xiao Zhang said: "No problem, just give me the key."
I said: "Thank you, sorry for the trouble."
A week later, I came back, and discovered the flowers on the balcony had bloomed beautifully.
I bought Xiao Zhang some fruit, and said once more: "Sorry for the trouble."
Xiao Zhang held the fruit and said: "Next time you go on a trip, just call on me."
I'm a northerner, but last year I moved to a city in the south because of work.
When I first arrived, I really wasn't used to the weather or the food here.
Winters in the north are very cold and it often snows, but in the south winter often brings rain and it rarely snows.
The food is different too: northerners love noodles, while southerners love rice.
People here speak very fast; at first I could hardly understand what they were saying.
But this city is clean and quiet, with lots of parks and a wonderful environment.
Slowly, I came to like it here more and more, and I made many warm-hearted southern friends.
Now when friends ask me whether the south or the north is better, I say with a smile: "Both are good, because both are home to me."
The first time I ate with chopsticks, I ate extremely slowly.
My friend Xiao Wang said, "Don't worry — let me tell you the story of chopsticks."
Long, long ago, people's food was very hot and couldn't be picked up by hand, so they used two small twigs to eat — these were the earliest chopsticks.
Chinese people have been using chopsticks for several thousand years; adults and small children can all use them.
There are also some table customs — for example, you must not stand your chopsticks in the rice.
When I first started practicing, every time I picked up food with my chopsticks, it always fell right back onto the plate.
I practiced at home every day, and after a week, I could really use chopsticks.
Now Xiao Wang says with a laugh, "You use chopsticks even better than I do!"
I used to take the bus to work; the roads were full of cars and I was often late.
A coworker asked me, "Why don't you take the subway?"
I tried it once and found the subway is both fast and cheap.
From home to the office takes only twenty minutes — much faster than the bus.
On the subway I can read a book or listen to music.
The subway station is very clean, and everyone lines up to board.
Last week it rained hard and the cars on the road moved especially slowly, but the subway was still fast.
Now I take the subway to work every day and haven't been late once — the subway is so convenient!
The son is going to work in the north, and mom helps him pack his suitcase.
Mom said: "It's cold in the north, you need to wear more clothes and take care of your health."
At the train station, mom still felt a little worried, and kept looking at her son.
The train was about to leave, and the son, holding his suitcase, said to his mother: "Mom, I'm heading off."
Mom said: "Call me once you arrive, look after yourself well, take care!"
The son said: "Mom, take care too, and don't worry about me."
The train pulled away, and his mother stood there watching it until she couldn't see it any more.
Last night, my friend and I went to a restaurant and ordered a lot of dishes.
We ate for a long time and were both full, but there was still a lot of food left on the table.
My friend said: "So much food — it'd be too wasteful not to finish it."
I said to the waiter: "We can't finish it all — can we get it packed to go?"
The waiter said: "Of course, I'll pack it up for you right away."
The waiter quickly packed up all the leftover food, and we carried it out of the restaurant.
Back home, I put the packed food on the table, planning to eat it again tomorrow at noon.
On Sunday, my friend Xiao Zhang took me to a very old teahouse.
His grandpa often drinks tea there. Grandpa said, "In China, drinking tea is not just drinking water — it is also a culture."
There are many kinds of Chinese tea; green tea and black tea are both very famous.
Grandpa taught me how to pour tea: when pouring tea for a guest, don't fill the cup too full.
He said with a smile, "If the cup is too full, it becomes hard for the guest to pick up."
We drank tea while listening to Grandpa's stories about the past, and the whole afternoon slipped by quickly.
The first cup of tea was a little hot, so I drank it slowly — but the more I drank, the better it tasted.
When I was leaving, Grandpa gave me a little tea and said, "The teahouse door is open every day — you're welcome to come often!"
This morning, I received an email; it was written by my manager.
The email said that I needed to send him the plan before five o'clock this afternoon.
I checked the time; there were only three hours left, and I felt a little anxious.
I immediately started writing the plan, checking it as I went.
After I finished writing, I read it over once more and found no mistakes.
At four thirty, I sent the plan to my manager.
Five minutes later, my manager sent me a message: 'Thank you, this is written very well!'
I finally felt relieved, and I was very happy inside.
At nine o'clock this morning, the company had an important meeting.
I got to the company very early to prepare things for the meeting.
When the meeting started, Xiao Wang hadn't arrived yet, and the manager was a little unhappy.
Ten minutes later, Xiao Wang finally ran in, saying sorry while sitting down.
We discussed next month's work plan at the meeting.
The manager said this plan was important, and hoped everyone would work hard to do it well.
After the meeting ended, we all felt this meeting was very useful.
Last month a few friends and I took a three-hour bus ride to go and see the pandas.
The panda is China's most famous animal, and many people come to China simply in order to see them.
It was drizzling that morning, but there were still an awful lot of people in the park.
We waited half an hour and finally saw a little panda.
It sat on the grass eating bamboo and watching us, not the least bit afraid.
I noticed that pandas walk very slowly, but they are extremely fast when they climb trees.
Books say that a giant panda has to spend more than ten hours a day eating bamboo.
There are more and more pandas in China now, and I hope that one day my children will be able to see them too.
Last Friday, my friend invited me to a restaurant for dinner, because it was her birthday.
I left home at five o'clock and got into a taxi.
At first the car went fast, but suddenly the cars in front all stopped moving — a traffic jam!
The driver said: "Today is Friday, and it's raining too, so there are especially many cars on the road."
We waited half an hour and the car only moved a little; I got more and more anxious.
I took a look at the map, found there was a subway station nearby, and got out of the taxi.
I first took the subway, then walked for ten minutes, and finally arrived at the restaurant at six thirty.
My friend said with a smile: "Great, you're not late!" I thought, next time I'd better just take the subway.
Last month I found a new job, so this Saturday I treated my friends to dinner.
We went to a restaurant near my company; the food there is both tasty and cheap.
I looked at the menu first and ordered six dishes and some beer for everyone.
My friend Xiao Li doesn't drink beer; he only asked for a glass of sweet fruit juice.
We chatted while eating, and everyone was very happy.
After the meal, my friends wanted to pay, but I said with a smile: "Today it's my treat — I won't take anyone's money!"
They said next time they would treat me, and that's what we decided.
Near my home there's a park, and the park has many old trees.
But in the last two years, the park has had fewer and fewer trees.
The environment has become not so good; there are also fewer birds than before.
In order to make the environment better, the school decided to take everyone to the park to plant trees.
Saturday morning, the classmates all brought young trees and happily went to the park.
When they arrived at the park, everyone planted many young trees together.
The teacher said that with more trees, the park will become more and more beautiful, and there will be more and more birds too.
After planting the trees, everyone was tired, but looking at the young trees, they felt happy inside.
This morning, my bike suddenly broke.
I checked the time — only ten minutes until class, and I got anxious.
I called a classmate and said: "My bike broke — what should I do?"
He said: "Don't worry — the bus stop isn't far from here, you can take the bus."
I hurried to the bus stop, and the bus came quickly.
After getting on, there was still a seat — I sat down, and slowly felt less nervous.
By the time I got to school, there were still two minutes before class — I wasn't late.
At lunch I treated my classmate to a meal, to thank him for the morning.
In the evening, a few of us friends wanted to eat together, but we didn't know where to go.
I asked everyone: "What do you want to eat?" Everyone said: "Whatever, anything's fine."
We walked into a restaurant, and the waiter let us find our own seats. I asked my friends where to sit, and they still said "whatever."
The waiter brought the menu and asked what we wanted to drink. My friends said again: "Whatever, you just order."
I looked over the menu and realized that everything, from where to sit to what to eat, was being decided by me alone.
So I ordered a few dishes everyone usually eats, plus a soup, and handed the menu back to the waiter.
When the food arrived, everyone ate happily, and nobody said "whatever" again.
I was shopping at a store for a long time, and suddenly I needed to use the restroom.
I asked a clerk: "Excuse me, where is the restroom?"
The clerk said: "Walk straight ahead, then turn left, and you'll be there."
I said thank you, and walked straight ahead.
After walking for a while, I saw a door with the three characters for "restroom" written on it.
I went through the door and finally found the restroom.
After I came out, I saw the clerk again — she smiled and asked me: "Did you find it?" I said: "I found it, thank you."
Recently there has been an awful lot going on at the company, and I have had to work overtime almost every day.
At eight o'clock last night, there were only two people in the office: me and the manager.
He asked me to finish writing all these emails, and then he sat down at his own computer and worked too.
I worked while listening to music; by the time I finished, it was already half past ten.
As I walked out of the company, there were fewer and fewer people on the street, and I felt both tired and hungry.
I bought a bowl of noodles at the supermarket downstairs, then sat on a bench in the park and ate slowly.
At that moment it suddenly hit me: money matters, but my health and my own time matter even more.
So I decided that from now on, except when things are especially busy, I will not work this late any more.
Next week we have an exam, and I'm very worried.
This exam is important, because it can decide my grade.
Every night, I review until very late before going to sleep.
As soon as I think about the exam, I feel nervous, and I don't sleep well at night either.
My friend told me: "Don't worry, you've already prepared very well."
Although I'm still a little scared, I decided to rest well and stop studying.
Tomorrow I'm about to take the exam, and I hope there's no problem.
Last winter I found my trousers getting tighter and tighter, so I decided to go work out at a gym.
On day one, I excitedly signed up for a one-year card and even bought new sports shoes.
The coach said that to see results, you must come at least three times a week.
For the first two weeks I went every day, and was so sore I couldn't even climb the stairs.
Later, when the weather turned cold, I started finding all kinds of excuses: it's raining today, overtime tomorrow, and the day after — we'll see.
Three months later, the gym called to ask whether I had lost my card.
Embarrassed, I went back — this time not demanding that I go every day, only that I train seriously each time.
Now I understand: signing up is easy, keeping at it is hard; getting fit takes a habit, not that card.
Many students find Chinese characters hard when they first start, and some even want to give up.
But as a Chinese teacher, I want to tell you: behind every character there is a little story.
The earliest characters were much like pictures: 山 looks like three mountain peaks, and the four dots inside 雨 look like falling rain.
When characters combine, the meanings get even more interesting: a person (人) leaning against a tree (木) makes 休 — the xiu of 休息, "to rest".
Characters are not only useful, they can also become art — Chinese people call the art of writing characters "shufa", calligraphy.
There is no secret to learning characters: the more you write, the more clearly you remember them.
Even if you learn only three to five characters a day, a year later you will still know more than a thousand.
So don't worry — one day you'll find that you are not memorizing characters, but getting to know an ancient culture.
On weekends at home, many people like to binge-watch episode after episode — once they start, it's a whole day.
The scariest thing while binge-watching is getting halfway through and suddenly finding there's no next episode.
TV dramas today are increasingly good, and the stories are more and more interesting, making people unable to resist wanting to know what happens next.
Some people feel binge-watching is a good way to relax — after finishing an episode, their stress is a little less.
But some people forget the time the moment they start binge-watching — they originally only wanted to watch one episode, but ended up watching until midnight.
The next day at work with no energy, they finally regret staying up so late watching the night before.
I don't think binge-watching itself is wrong — you just should set a time limit for yourself and go to sleep once you're done.
After all, resting well is also so that you can live better the next day.
In China, many parents worry about their children's marriage prospects, so they arrange blind dates for them.
A blind date is when your parents or friends introduce you to someone you don't know yet, to see if you're a good match.
Many young people are unwilling to go on blind dates at first, feeling that it's too restrictive.
But as they get older and busier with work, opportunities to meet new friends become fewer and fewer.
So quite a few people also start to accept the blind dates their parents arrange.
During a blind date, the two people will usually eat and chat together, getting to know each other a little.
If the two of them get along, they can continue seeing each other; if there's no chemistry, they don't need to meet again.
I think blind dates aren't a bad thing — they just give you one more chance to meet someone new.
In China's big cities, fewer and fewer people use cash.
Buying groceries, taking the bus, seeing a doctor — as long as you take out your phone and scan, the payment is done in a few seconds.
Last month I went traveling, and I never opened my wallet even once.
Not carrying cash is of course convenient, and safer too — they say even thieves are about to be out of a job.
But a cashless society has problems too: many elderly people don't know how to pay by phone and get really anxious when shopping.
And when your phone runs out of battery, you can't even buy a bottle of water.
Despite these problems, I still think going cashless is a direction that won't change.
Technology should wait a bit for those who walk more slowly, instead of leaving them behind.
This May I went to Lijiang in Yunnan, an ancient town with more than eight hundred years of history.
There are no cars in the old town, only quiet old streets and crystal-clear water that flows along the side of every street.
During the day I strolled along the old streets, and when I got tired I would find a teahouse, sit down, and watch the tourists come and go.
In good weather you can see the snow mountain in the distance right from town; under the blue sky, its snow shines bright white.
At night Lijiang is a completely different place: lights and music everywhere, as lively as a festival.
There I got to know an old man who runs a small inn; he said he has lived in Lijiang his whole life and has never once thought of leaving.
He said with a smile: 'Cities get faster and faster, but Lijiang has always been slow — slow is simply our way of life.'
On the morning I left, I thought: what makes Lijiang so charming is not only its beautiful scenery, but also the kind of life that makes people slow down.
After graduating from university, everyone runs into an important question: what kind of career to choose.
My parents hope I will become a teacher, because the job is stable and the pressure is low.
But I am especially interested in computer technology and want to go to a big city to find a job related to the internet.
A friend told me that when choosing a career, salary matters of course, but interest matters even more.
If you spend every day doing things you don't like, no salary, however high, can make you happy.
I thought for a long time and decided to first try working at an internet company to gain some experience.
Although Mom and Dad were a little disappointed, in the end they still supported my decision.
A career is just like a pair of shoes: only your own feet know whether it fits.
A dozen or so years ago, few people in China drank coffee; everyone preferred tea.
But now, as life changes, more and more coffee shops are opening in every city.
For many young people, coffee is not just a drink.
The first cup in the morning is how work begins; the afternoon cup is a small gift to yourself.
Interestingly, coffee in China has developed its own flavor — coffee with tea, coffee with fruit.
Some say drinking coffee is copying Westerners; I feel, however, that Chinese people have turned coffee into a culture of their own.
Actually, neither tea nor coffee is better than the other — what matters is the moment you sit down and drink slowly.
Many young people are busy all day; only the evening hours belong to themselves.
So they don't want to sleep; they scroll on their phones while telling themselves, "Just ten more minutes."
As a result, ten minutes turns into two hours, and by the time they go to bed it is already the middle of the night.
Staying up late seems to give us a little freedom, but really it is borrowing time from our own body.
What you borrow must always be paid back: the next day your head hurts, you have no energy at work, and you can't do anything well.
I used to stay up late all the time too; not until I got sick and was hospitalized did I understand how important health is.
Now I go to bed at eleven every night, and when I get up in the morning the whole world feels brand new.
Go to bed a little earlier tonight — tomorrow's you will thank today's you.
Nowadays, ordering food delivery has already become part of many people's lives.
As long as you pick your dishes on your phone, half an hour later hot food arrives at your door.
Delivery is fast and convenient; it lets us skip cooking and skip going out.
But behind the convenience there is also a price.
Some people discover they haven't set foot in the kitchen for a whole year.
To be a little faster, delivery riders often ride dangerously.
I think it's fine to order delivery, but on weekends it's best to cook a meal yourself.
Because cooking is not only about eating — it is also the flavor of life itself.
In China, 'face' is an extremely important word.
Face is not your actual face, but how other people see you.
When friends eat out together, everyone often fights to pay the bill — whoever pays gains face.
If you criticize someone in front of many people, he will feel he has lost face and may never want to be your friend again.
So when Chinese people give feedback, they like to put it politely — strengths first, problems second.
Some people find caring too much about face exhausting — treating guests and giving gifts all cost a lot of money.
I think face is like clothing: worn right, it makes people comfortable; worn in too many layers, you get unbearably hot.
My best friend is Li Jing; we have known each other since primary school and grew up together.
Three years ago she moved abroad with her husband, and suddenly there were eight thousand kilometers between us.
At first I felt awful, worried that our friendship would slowly fade away.
The time over there is exactly the opposite of here: when I am having breakfast, she is getting ready for bed.
But we made a deal: no matter how busy we are, we video call once every weekend, and neither of us is allowed to forget.
When she is feeling down, I will drag myself out of bed to chat with her, even if it is the middle of the night.
Last winter she came back, and the moment we saw each other we burst out laughing, as if we had never been apart.
Now I understand: even if true friends are far apart, their hearts stay close.
Last week, I went to see a Traditional Chinese Medicine doctor for the first time.
The TCM doctor first took my pulse, then asked whether I had been sleeping well lately.
He said I was under too much stress and not sleeping enough at night, so my body was a bit weak.
The doctor prescribed some Chinese herbal medicine for me and told me to drink it once a day.
The medicine tasted very bitter, but after drinking it for a few days, I felt much more comfortable.
I also tried acupuncture — it hurt a little at first, but I got used to it afterward.
A friend told me that seeing a TCM doctor requires patience, since the effects aren't visible right away.
This experience gave me a new understanding of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
Every year when December arrives, seats become hard to find in many university libraries, because the day of the grad school entrance exam is approaching.
According to statistics, several million college students now register for the graduate entrance exam every year, and the number keeps rising year after year.
Some students are genuinely interested in academics and hope to continue in-depth research through graduate study.
However, quite a few others are only treating the grad exam as a "temporary way out" because finding a job is too hard.
Since an undergraduate degree is no longer enough, many people feel that only by pursuing graduate study can they become more competitive.
But the grad exam is not at all easy — it requires spending more than ten hours a day memorizing texts and doing practice questions, which brings huge stress.
Some people have even given up their original interests because of too much stress, which makes people wonder: what is graduate study really for?
I think, whether for an ideal or for finding a job, what matters is being clear about what you truly want.
Last month I went to Beijing with a few colleagues to climb the Great Wall.
I had seen the Great Wall many times in photos before, and thought I already knew it well.
But when I actually stood beneath the Great Wall, I was still moved: it looked like a long dragon climbing from one mountain to the next, with no end in sight.
Some stretches of the wall are really hard to walk; we had climbed less than halfway before we were so tired we had to sit down and rest.
One colleague joked, 'Let's just sit here and wait for the Great Wall to walk over to us!' Everyone laughed, and after the laugh we encouraged each other and kept climbing.
Near the highest point, my legs ached so much I could hardly lift them, and I really wanted to give up.
But then I thought: hundreds of years ago, people did not even have machines, yet they left behind such a great structure on mountains this high — so I had no reason to stop.
When I finally stood at the highest point and watched the wall slowly disappear into the distant clouds, I was too moved to speak.
On the way down I told my colleagues that sticking it out the whole way had truly been worth it.
In recent years, more and more young people have been strolling and taking photos on the streets while wearing hanfu.
The long sleeves and exquisite patterns make people think of ancient poetry and stories at first glance.
For quite a few young people, wearing hanfu is not only about looking good, but also a way of expressing love for traditional culture.
However, some people question: do these people really understand the history behind hanfu, or are they only doing it to take good-looking photos?
In fact, a genuine hanfu takes great care from the fabric to the tailoring — it is definitely not something you can just casually put on.
So, some enthusiasts have started seriously studying ancient clothing, and even make the clothes themselves.
Since young people are willing to spend time and money to understand traditional culture, this in itself is something worth encouraging.
I think, whether out of love for history or love for photography, the hanfu craze has let more people rediscover the beauty of traditional culture.
Twenty years ago, the train from Beijing to Shanghai took more than ten hours.
Now the high-speed train takes only four and a half hours.
The high-speed train is fast and safe, the seats are comfortable, and the carriages are quiet.
You can drink tea and read on board, watching cities and mountains fly past the window.
What high-speed rail has changed is not only speed, but also people's lives.
Many people live in one city and work in another; going home by high-speed train on weekends to see their parents has also become easy.
Some people say the world has become smaller.
Actually the world hasn't changed — it is the distance between us and faraway places that has grown shorter.
Summer vacation is coming soon, and my friend and I have been discussing our holiday plans.
I want to go south to see the ocean, because summer in the north is too hot.
My friend thinks traveling is too tiring — he prefers staying home to read and sleep in.
Our ideas are completely different, and neither of us can persuade the other.
In the end, we decided to each arrange our own vacation and not bother each other.
I booked my flight and hotel, planning to spend a week at the seaside.
Before leaving, I arranged all my work so that I could rest with peace of mind.
I think that no matter how you spend a vacation, what matters most is truly letting yourself relax.
In China, hotpot is not only a way of eating, but also a great chance to get together with friends.
As soon as the weather turns cold, I want to round up a few old friends and go eat hotpot together.
One table, one steaming pot — everyone drops in meat and vegetables, eating and chatting at the same time.
While eating hotpot, almost nobody looks at their phone, because everyone is busy fishing tasty things out of the pot.
Some people love spicy food and some are afraid of it — no problem, the pot can be split in two: one half spicy, one half mild.
For me, the taste of hotpot is the taste of friendship — the livelier the table, the warmer my heart.
Even if work is ever so busy, we should still sit down with friends often and enjoy a slow hotpot meal.
Because the most delicious thing has never been what's in the pot, but the people sitting beside you.
Chinese has many "chengyu" — idioms — and behind each one there is a story; today let's look at the story of 画蛇添足, "drawing a snake and adding feet".
Long ago, a few men were given a pot of good wine, but there was too little of it — only enough for one person.
So they decided on a contest: each would draw a snake on the ground, and whoever finished first would get the wine.
One man drew extremely fast; seeing that the others were still not done, he said smugly: "I still have time — let me add a few feet to my snake!"
But just as he was drawing the feet, another man finished his snake, picked up the wine pot and said: "A snake has no feet to begin with — what on earth did you draw?"
With that, he drank the wine — while the man who had drawn fastest ended up with nothing at all.
Ever since, people have used 画蛇添足 for situations like this: something was already fine, yet someone insisted on doing something useless, and as a result made it worse.
It's the same with study and work: sometimes doing more doesn't necessarily mean doing better — knowing when to stop is a kind of wisdom too.
When looking for a job, the interview is often more important than the resume.
Many people are quite capable, yet because they get too nervous, they can't get a single sentence out well in the interview.
Actually, there are techniques to interviewing.
First, before you go, learn about the company and find out what kind of person they need.
Second, when answering questions, don't just say "I work very hard" — it's best to give a real example.
In addition, dress neatly and arrive ten minutes early — these small things all leave a good impression.
Finally, don't forget: an interview is not only the company choosing you, but also you choosing the company.
Relax a little, treat the interview as a chat, and you will do even better.
Speaking of Chinese movies, the first thing many foreigners think of is kung fu movies.
From Bruce Lee to Jackie Chan, these actors made the world know about Chinese kung fu.
In kung fu movies, the protagonist often goes from an ordinary person, through hard work, to become someone truly formidable.
Stories like this make people feel that as long as you keep practicing, anyone can become stronger.
Besides fighting, kung fu movies also often talk about friendship, family, and responsibility.
Although young people today prefer to watch other movies, there are still many people willing to watch old kung fu films again.
For me, the most interesting thing about kung fu movies is the simple truth that "if you work hard, you can become strong."
Maybe that's why, even decades later, kung fu movies are still so popular.
Last summer, I finally signed up to learn how to drive.
The first time I sat in the instructor's car, my hands were shaking from nervousness.
The instructor was very patient, teaching me step by step how to handle the steering wheel and step on the brake.
While practicing, I kept nervously mistaking the gas pedal for the brake.
The instructor said with a smile, don't worry, take it slow, everyone learns this way.
After practicing for two months, I could finally do reverse parking smoothly.
On the day of the test, my heart was beating especially fast, but in the end I passed smoothly.
Looking back now, learning to drive not only taught me how to drive, but also taught me the importance of patience.
Open your phone, and at any time you can see someone in a livestream room introducing products, talking and selling at the same time.
The host's voice is fast and excited, and often just one line — "last three minutes" — makes many people place an order right away.
The biggest advantage of livestream shopping is that it's cheap, because it saves on the costs of shops and middlemen.
Moreover, you can watch the host try out the product while asking questions, which feels more reassuring than just looking at pictures online.
However, some people are still watching livestreams deep into the night, and before they know it, they've bought a pile of things they don't need at all.
What's even more worrying is that a few hosts exaggerate product effects in order to sell goods, and even sell fake products.
Since livestream shopping has already become a shopping habit, consumers need to stay even more rational and not get carried away by the atmosphere.
When it comes down to it, livestream shopping itself is not the problem — the problem is whether we are clear about what we truly need.
Last month I bought a notebook and decided to manage my time seriously.
On the first day I wrote down twelve things to do, and in the end finished only three.
Later I realised the problem wasn't a lack of time, but that I always did the easy things first.
Replying to messages, tidying my desk — after doing those I felt busy, but in fact I hadn't done a single important thing.
So I changed my method: each morning I write down only the three most important things.
What's more, I put my phone in another room and don't look at it even once before noon.
Two weeks later, although I finish fewer things each day, every one of them is the most important kind.
A colleague said I look more relaxed than before; in fact I have simply learned to say no to some things.
Time management is not about making yourself do more things, but about making yourself do the right things.
In China, people speak Mandarin at school and at work, but the moment they get home, what many of them speak is their dialect.
A dialect is a region's own way of speaking — Shanghainese or Cantonese, for example — and the difference from Mandarin can sometimes be huge.
My grandma can only speak our hometown dialect; the moment she opens her mouth, I feel a special warmth.
Mandarin lets people from different places communicate easily, and that of course is very important.
But nowadays, many children who grow up in cities surprisingly can no longer understand their grandparents' dialect.
Some people worry that in a few more decades, certain dialects may slowly disappear.
Actually, we don't have to choose between Mandarin and dialects: Mandarin helps us go farther, while dialects remind us where we come from.
If you travel in China, learn a few phrases of the local dialect besides Mandarin — the locals are sure to be especially warm to you.
It has already been ten years since I left my hometown.
When I first came to this big city, I assumed I would go back very soon.
Later, a job, friends, someone I love — one by one, they kept me here.
Every Spring Festival I take a twenty-hour train home, and my mother is always waiting for me at the door.
Her cooking still tastes the same, but her hair has turned so much whiter.
The city gave me a new life, yet my hometown keeps my oldest memories.
When someone asks me, "Where is your home?" — I cannot answer clearly.
Perhaps that is what a migrant is: someone who lives in a new place, but has left their heart somewhere far away.
As soon as evening falls, the old streets in many cities become lively, because the night market has begun.
Whether you want to eat snacks or buy cheap clothes, the night market can satisfy you.
What I like best is that fragrance in the air where fried chicken and grilled meat mix together.
What's interesting is that the night market is not just a place to eat and shop, but also a place for young people to take photos, chat, and go on dates.
Since everyone is at work or school during the day, coming out to relax in the evening has become a lifestyle habit.
However, as cities become more and more modernized, some old night markets are slowly disappearing due to redevelopment.
So, some people have begun to worry: if all night markets turn into shopping malls, will that lively yet warm feeling still be found?
I think what a night market represents is not just delicious food, but the character of a city at night.
Many people think friends made online are all fake, and I used to think so too.
Last year I joined an online reading group and got to know someone called 'Little Fish'.
Every week we discussed the same book, and the more we chatted, the more I found our personalities to be remarkably alike.
Of course, making friends online has its dangers: you cannot see the person you are chatting with, and you don't know whether what they say is true or false.
That is why I never tell online friends my address, and never casually lend anyone money.
Six months later, Little Fish came to my city on a business trip, and we arranged to meet at a café.
Before we met I was really nervous, afraid the real her would be completely different from the online her — but it turned out she was, amazingly, exactly as I had imagined.
We chatted for an entire afternoon, from books to work, and from work to life.
I think the internet is just one way of meeting people; whether a friendship is real depends, in the end, on whether both people are honest.
Last year I saw a puppy at a friend's house; it was so cute and clever that I decided on the spot I wanted one too.
But only after bringing the puppy home did I discover that keeping a pet is not as simple as I had imagined.
Every morning at six it wakes me up, and no matter whether it is windy or raining, I have to take it out for a walk.
When it gets sick I have to take it to the vet — one visit once cost more than a thousand yuan.
When I want to go traveling, I first have to find a friend willing to look after it; otherwise I can only give up the plan.
For a while I was genuinely exhausted, and I even slightly regretted getting it.
But every day when I come home, it runs over happily to greet me, and in that moment all the hard work becomes worth it.
Now I often tell friends who want a pet: a pet is not a toy but a life, and only if you can take responsibility for it should you bring one home.
Nowadays, the phone has become one of the most important things in our lives.
We use our phones to chat, shop, read the news — even to work.
But more and more people find they can't live without their phones.
They look at their phones while eating, and again before going to sleep.
I think we should put down our phones and spend more time with family and friends.
Every evening, familiar music starts playing right on time in the park, and a group of aunties begin dancing plaza dance.
Their movements are simple, but they dance in perfect unison, and they look very happy.
Plaza dancing not only exercises the body, but also adds a lot of joy to life after retirement.
But the music is too loud, making people who live nearby feel both noisy and annoyed.
So, plaza dancing has slowly become a controversial topic: is it a healthy activity, or is it disturbing the residents?
Some communities have come up with solutions, such as setting rules for dancing hours and volume, which has gradually reduced the conflict.
When it comes down to it, plaza dancing reflects elderly people's longing to socialize and to be seen.
I think, as long as everyone understands each other, plaza dancing can completely become a warm scene in the city.
Open the music app on your phone, and everywhere you look there are pleasant pop songs.
Before, people had to buy songs to listen to them; now, as long as you go online, you can hear almost every song there is.
Pop song lyrics mostly talk about love, life, or the worries of young people, making people feel that what's sung in the song is their own story.
Some singers sing beautifully and are also good at writing lyrics, so they quickly become famous.
But some people also worry that many songs today are too short and too fast-paced, as if they exist only to get people to replay them online more times.
I myself like old songs best — the kind with simple lyrics that you still enjoy even after listening to them for many years.
Pop music keeps changing, but people's desire to express their feelings through songs has never changed.
Long ago, there was a man who was extremely good at archery — he could hit the target nine times out of ten, and so he was very proud.
One day, an old oil seller stood nearby watching him shoot, and gave only a slight nod.
Annoyed, the man asked, "Do you really think my archery is not good?"
The old man said, "It is nothing special — you have simply practiced a lot."
With that, the old man set a bottle on the ground and placed on top of it a copper coin with a small hole in the middle.
Slowly he poured the oil through the small hole into the bottle, and not a drop of oil touched the coin.
The old man said with a smile, "I am nothing special either — I have simply poured oil many, many times."
The man understood: with anything at all, as long as you do it and practice it enough, you can do it both quickly and well.
This is what "practice makes perfect" means.
In today's China, a tiny QR code has changed almost every aspect of life.
Groceries, buses, restaurants, the doctor — as long as you take out your phone and scan, the payment is done in an instant.
In restaurants, the waiter no longer hands you a menu, but instead asks you to scan the QR code on the table to order.
The first time my grandma used a QR code to buy something, she was so nervous her hands were sweating.
Later she mastered it — nowadays even the old man selling fruit downstairs uses a QR code to collect money.
Of course, behind the convenience there are problems too: some elderly people have no smartphone, and shopping becomes very difficult for them.
So now many shops have a sign at the entrance: "Cash welcome."
New technology should make everyone's life more convenient, rather than convenient for only some people.
In China's big cities, queuing is one of the most common things in life: you queue to shop, you queue for the bus, and you queue at the hospital too.
Some people are very patient in line, looking at their phones while slowly waiting.
But some people don't want to wait: seeing many people ahead, they simply cut in line.
People who cut in line may think they are clever, but actually everyone silently resents them.
I once saw an elderly man politely say to a young man who had cut in line: "We are all waiting — would you please go to the back?"
The young man blushed, said "sorry," and immediately went to stand at the end of the line.
Queuing seems like a small matter, but it actually best shows a place's level of civility.
If you are willing to wait three minutes, others will be willing to wait three minutes for you too.
China is huge — when people from different places speak Mandarin, each may carry a little accent of their own.
For example, some southern friends can't tell "si" (four) from "shi" (ten); when they say "forty", listeners often have to think for a second.
When I first went to Beijing for university, the moment my classmates heard me talk, they would ask with a smile: "You're from the south, right?"
Back then I felt a bit embarrassed, and didn't even really want to speak up in class.
Later a teacher said to me: "An accent is not a flaw — it shows you have a hometown of your own."
Now I find that accents make a language richer, just as the same dish tastes different in different places.
For you as a Chinese learner, there's no need to fear your own accent either — as long as people can understand you, you're already speaking well.
The more you dare to speak up, the faster you improve — and that matters far more than perfect pronunciation.
Last month I changed jobs, and the new company was too far from my old home, so I decided to rent a place near the office.
There was plenty of information online, but some photos were completely different from the real thing.
I looked at five apartments; they were either too expensive or too old.
Finally I found a suitable room, only one stop from the office, with a clean kitchen and bathroom.
The landlord was a friendly auntie who said: "The rent is two thousand a month, and you pay for water and electricity yourself."
I discussed with her whether it could be a bit cheaper, and she smiled and agreed to charge one hundred kuai less per month.
When signing the contract, I carefully read through every single clause.
The evening I moved into my new home, I felt both tired and happy, as if life were starting all over again.
Old Wang has been driving for a ride-hailing app for three years, running around the city for over ten hours every day.
He says that when there's traffic during the day, a single trip can sometimes take an hour.
Last night, a female passenger got in the car and cried on the phone the whole time.
Old Wang didn't ask her what was wrong — he just turned the air conditioner a bit warmer and drove quietly.
When they arrived, the passenger said thank you before getting out, and her mood seemed to have improved a little.
Old Wang says with a smile that the most interesting part of driving is meeting different people and stories every day.
He also admits the job is tiring and the income isn't very stable — the good days and bad days are very different.
But he feels that hearing so many strangers' stories is also a kind of gain.
Last month when I was moving, I took some things I no longer needed to the secondhand market to sell.
The secondhand market has everything — from old clothes and old books to old furniture, it's all there.
Sellers set a price that isn't too high, and buyers can haggle further.
I sold an almost-unused desk to a college student who had just moved in.
He said buying secondhand things saves money and is eco-friendly, since you don't have to wait for factories to make new ones.
I myself found an old-fashioned chair at the market, whose look was quite special.
Even though it's secondhand, if the quality is good, using it feels almost the same as something new.
Now I like browsing the secondhand market more and more, because behind every item there's a story.
Have you noticed that things in ads always look prettier than the real ones?
The hamburger in the photo is big and fresh, but once you buy it and take a look, it's completely different.
Ads also like to fool people with numbers — for example, it says nine out of ten people say it's good, when actually it only asked ten people.
The cleverest trick is making you feel that everyone is buying it, because nobody wants to be the last one to buy.
I used to be fooled by ads all the time too, buying lots of things I never got to use.
Later I learned a trick: when I see something I like, I first wait three days before deciding.
Three days later, if I still want it, I buy it; most of the time, I have already forgotten about it.
The secret of advertising is actually simple: what it sells is not a product, but your dream.
A few years ago, shared bikes suddenly appeared on the streets of Chinese cities.
As long as you scan with your phone, you can ride a bike away — extremely convenient.
The subway station is still two kilometers from your office? Ten minutes by bike and you're there.
Shared bikes are not only cheap but also good for the environment, so many people stopped driving.
But problems came too: some people parked bikes in the middle of the road, and others even rode them home to keep.
Later, more and more bikes lay broken, and some streets looked like a "sea" of bicycles.
Shared bikes taught us something: a good idea still needs everyone to take care of it together.
Five years ago, the sky in many Chinese cities was rarely blue — smog was everywhere.
At that time, as soon as winter arrived, the air would get worse, and many people didn't dare go out to exercise.
When going out, everyone also had to wear a face mask, afraid of breathing in bad air.
In recent years, the situation has gotten much better.
The government shut down some factories with serious pollution, and also encouraged everyone to take public transportation more and drive less.
Now, in many cities, the number of days each year with blue sky keeps increasing.
I still remember, when I was small, my mom always made me put on a mask before I could go out and play — now, days like that are already rare.
There are more blue-sky days now, which shows that as long as everyone works hard together, the environment can improve.
Nowadays people's lives move faster and faster, and the stress keeps growing too.
Work, housing, the children's education — every single thing makes people tense.
Many people assume that as long as they work hard, they will get to live an easy life.
But they discover that the busier they get, the greater the stress — yet their happiness keeps shrinking.
Actually, relaxing is not wasting time — it is refueling yourself.
You can go out for a little walk, listen to some music, or have a chat with friends.
For me, the best way to relax is to turn off my phone in the evening and quietly read a book.
Remember: only when you have rested well can you go further.
At half past six every morning, there are already many elderly people practising tai chi in the park.
Their movements are slow — so slow it looks as if they were walking under water.
I always assumed tai chi was only exercise for old people — until the doctor told me to move around more.
One Saturday morning, I sheepishly took a place behind them.
An older man said to me: don't rush, first learn how to stand properly.
That morning we practised for only twenty minutes, but my legs were even more tired than after a run.
Now I understand: tai chi looks easy, but it is not simple at all.
After half a year of practice, I found that the slower the movements, the calmer I felt inside.
For young people today, slowing down may be even harder than running fast.
In China, gift giving is an art: what to give and how to give it both follow particular rules.
For example, when visiting a friend's home you can bring fruit, and the number had better be even, because even numbers represent good things.
Some things must not be given casually: clocks are out, and so are umbrellas, because their pronunciation makes people think of unlucky meanings.
My foreign friend was very surprised to hear this; he said that in his country, you can give anything.
Actually, a gift doesn't need to be expensive; what matters is your thoughtfulness.
Receiving gifts has its culture too: many Chinese people will first politely say "you shouldn't have," and only then accept.
In the past, many people would not open a gift right away; today's young people often open it while saying thank you.
What gift giving really gives is not just things, but even more the affection between people.
Within less than three hundred metres of my office building, five milk tea shops have opened.
Every day at three in the afternoon, my colleagues start discussing what to drink today.
One cup of milk tea costs about twenty yuan, even more expensive than a lunch.
Yet everyone is still willing to queue, sometimes waiting half an hour.
The owner says that what young people buy is not just a drink, but also a mood.
As more and more new shops opened, prices slowly came down too.
I did the maths: if I had one cup a day, I would spend more than seven thousand yuan a year.
Since it would cost that much in a year, I decided to have it only once a week.
Still, every time I walk past a milk tea shop, I can't help taking a look inside.
In China, asking someone's age can be a bit impolite, so people often first ask what zodiac animal you were born under.
The twelve zodiac signs are twelve animals, one animal per year; after twelve years it starts again from the first one.
I was born in the year of the horse, and so was my mother; we are exactly twenty-four years apart.
Every year at New Year, that year's animal is everywhere in the shops.
People say children born in the year of the dragon are especially welcome, so there are especially many babies born in dragon years.
I do think, though, that a person's character has little to do with the year they were born.
As long as you work hard, it makes no difference which animal year you were born in.
But I still like the question, because it instantly gives two people who have just met something to chat about.
The delivery station downstairs from my building opens as early as six every morning.
The rider who delivers the parcels is surnamed Wang, and everyone calls him Xiao Wang.
He not only remembers everyone's name, he also knows whose home is empty during the day.
No matter whether it's windy or raining, he shows up downstairs on time every day.
Once, when I was in a meeting, he left the box at my door and even sent me a text to let me know.
I asked him how many parcels he has to deliver in a day, and he said with a smile: more than two hundred.
For me, buying something online is just a tap on my phone; for him, it's a day of running from morning till night.
So now, whenever I take a parcel, I always make a point of saying a sincere thank you.
Since last year, where we live has required trash sorting, and at first everyone found it a huge hassle.
A banana peel, a plastic bag, a half-finished milk tea — which bin should each of them go into?
Aunt Wang from downstairs stands by the bins every day, inspecting everyone's trash the way a teacher checks homework.
Once I threw a battery into the wrong place, and she earnestly gave me a ten-minute lesson.
Slowly, I found that I really do stop and think first before throwing things away now.
Even more interesting, the trash at home has decreased, because before buying anything I have also started asking myself: do I really need this?
Trash sorting is a hassle, sure — but it has made us see our own lives anew.
Before my first trip alone, I was very worried: what if I got lost? What if I got sick?
My friends also said it wasn't safe for a girl to go off on her own.
But I bought a train ticket anyway and went to a small city in the south.
When you travel alone, no one makes decisions for you — where to go, what to eat, where to stay, you have to figure it all out yourself.
Sometimes I got lost and sometimes I took the wrong bus, but every single time warm-hearted people helped me.
When you are on your own, you notice the scenery along the way more, and you talk to strangers more easily.
When the trip ended, I discovered that I had gotten to know not only a new place, but also a new me.
It turns out I am braver than I thought.
The twenty-four solar terms are the twenty-four segments into which ancient Chinese people divided the year, based on the sun's position in the sky.
From "Start of Spring" to "Greater Cold," every solar term corresponds to changes in climate and crop growth.
In ancient times farmers relied on solar terms to arrange planting and harvesting; for instance, "around Tomb-Sweeping Day, plant melons and beans" is a farmers' proverb passed down to this day.
Besides guiding agriculture, solar terms also deeply influence Chinese people's daily life and eating habits.
For example, on the day of Winter Solstice, northerners are used to eating dumplings, while southerners prefer to eat sweet rice balls.
As urbanization has developed, although many people no longer work in agriculture, solar terms still appear in calendars and weather forecasts.
Interestingly, as early as 2016 the twenty-four solar terms were included by UNESCO on the list of human intangible cultural heritage.
This shows that ancient wisdom has not lost its value because of changing times — on the contrary, it continues on in new forms.
As medical science develops, people are living longer and longer, and there are more and more elderly people in society.
Many countries are entering an "aging society," and this has already become an important social issue.
The more elderly people there are, the more people are needed to care for them, so naturally the pressure on young people grows too.
At the same time, with more people retired and fewer people working, the country's economic development will also be affected.
However, an aging population is not entirely a bad thing.
Many elderly people are healthy and rich in experience, and after retiring they can continue to contribute to society.
Some experts suggest raising the retirement age, while others suggest encouraging young people to have more children.
No matter what methods we use, we should respect the elderly and let them live happy, joyful lives.
Recently our company started using artificial intelligence to write reports, and my colleagues' reactions have been very different.
Some worry their jobs will be replaced by machines, while others feel they can finally work less overtime.
To be honest, I have both feelings.
The AI really is faster than me: it takes me two hours to write a summary, and it can finish one in two minutes.
But it also makes mistakes often, and it gets things wrong with such confidence that you simply cannot notice unless you check carefully.
So my job has slowly changed: before, I did the writing; now, I judge whether the machine wrote it correctly.
A senior colleague said that in history, every time a new technology appeared people feared unemployment, yet in the end new professions always emerged.
Those words may well be true, but the road from the old job to the new one often takes many years to walk.
I don't know what I will be doing ten years from now; all I can do is keep learning while I use these tools.
The Tang dynasty, more than one thousand three hundred years ago, was the golden age of Chinese poetry.
At that time, almost everyone could write poems: emperors wrote them, soldiers wrote them, and even wine sellers wrote them.
The Complete Tang Poems preserves nearly fifty thousand poems, by more than two thousand authors.
The beauty of Tang poetry lies first of all in its sound: every poem is like a tiny song, and reading it aloud is especially pleasant.
Secondly, the poets were good at using the simplest characters to express the deepest feelings.
For example, when they missed home, they did not say "I am sad", but instead wrote about the moon, or about autumn leaves.
Today, the first poem Chinese children memorize after starting school is still usually a Tang poem.
In the smartphone era, many young people turn Tang poems into music and short videos, and the ancient poems have come back to life.
Perhaps this is the beauty of Tang poetry: time keeps changing, yet human feelings have not.
Old Zhang is a taxi driver; he is fifty-eight this year and has already been donating blood for free for more than twenty years.
The first time he donated blood was the year he was twenty-six — he saw a blood donation van on the street and curiously walked in.
The nurse said his blood type is O, which can be given to almost any patient — this made him feel it was especially meaningful.
From then on, Old Zhang went to donate blood every few months; over more than twenty years, he has donated close to eighty times in total.
Someone asked him: "Doesn't donating blood affect your health?" Old Zhang said as long as you donate according to the regulated time and amount, there's no harm to your health.
He also said that before every blood draw, the nurse checks your body — if you don't meet the standard, they simply won't let you donate.
Old Zhang's blood has already helped many complete strangers — patients and new mothers — yet he himself has never once met them.
He said: "I don't know whose life my blood saved, but when I think that someone survived because of that bag of blood, I feel it's worth it."
Now his son also goes together with him, donating blood at the blood donation van every year.
In the eyes of Chinese people, writing characters is not merely recording language; it is, even more, an art, called calligraphy.
Calligraphers use a brush and ink to write characters in all kinds of styles on paper: some are as calm as a great mountain, others as free as flowing water.
In ancient times, as soon as children entered school, the first thing they had to learn was how to hold the brush.
People believe that "the writing is like the person": by looking at someone's handwriting, you can tell their personality.
The most famous calligrapher is Wang Xizhi, who lived more than one thousand six hundred years ago.
Legend says he practiced so diligently that the water from washing his brushes turned a whole pool by his door black.
Today, although everyone types on computers and phones, the number of people learning calligraphy has not decreased; on the contrary, it keeps growing.
Many foreign friends have also begun learning calligraphy; they say that while writing, the mind slowly calms down.
Just one brush and one sheet of paper can make a person put down the phone and enjoy a stretch of quiet time.
The first time I heard the term "carbon neutrality" was on the TV news, and to be honest, I understood none of it at the time.
Only after looking it up did I understand: simply put, however much carbon dioxide you emit, you must reduce or absorb that same amount, so the total equals zero.
China's goal is to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060, which means energy, transportation, and industry must all undergo enormous changes.
It sounds like something that concerns only governments and big companies, with little to do with ordinary people.
But think about it carefully: our everyday choices are actually all connected to it — drive or take the subway, turn on the air conditioner or open the window.
The buses below my building have all been switched to electric ones — so quiet that at first I couldn't even get used to it.
Of course, some people doubt it: if I alone use one less plastic bag, does it really make a difference?
One person's power is indeed small, but what policy can change is precisely the shared habits of hundreds of millions of people.
Even if all you do is turn off the lights when you leave, it still counts as taking part in this great undertaking whose results will only be visible decades from now.
On the night of Double Eleven, I had put more than thirty items in my shopping cart, and just before paying I suddenly asked myself: do I really need these?
Advertisements always tell us: buy this and you will be more beautiful, more successful, happier.
In a bad mood? Buy something. In a great mood? Then all the more reason to buy something to celebrate.
This is exactly what consumerism is: it turns shopping from satisfying needs into proving yourself.
I have a friend whose salary is not low, yet he spends it all every month, even borrowing money to buy the newest phone.
He says: "Everyone else has one and I don't — how embarrassing would that be."
The problem is, this kind of happiness comes fast and goes fast: after three weeks the new phone becomes just an ordinary old phone.
That night I turned off my phone and went to sleep first; the next day I looked at the cart again, and in the end kept only one pair of sneakers I truly needed.
After buying less, I did not feel my life got worse at all — on the contrary, I felt a great deal lighter.
With the advance of globalization, cross-national marriages have become more and more common in China.
My good friend Xiaoyu married a German engineer, and their story gave me a new understanding of marriage.
When they were newly married, cultural differences caused quite a few conflicts between them.
For example, Xiaoyu feels a couple's income should be pooled and managed together, while her husband believes it is more sensible for each to manage their own.
Whether to give red envelopes to the relatives' children at Spring Festival once kept them arguing for days.
Later they discovered that when disagreements arise, it is better to sit down and really communicate than to blame each other.
Xiaoyu often says: "Love brought us together, but what makes a marriage last is understanding and respect."
In my view, every marriage takes careful effort; a cross-national marriage merely magnifies the cultural differences, that's all.
As long as both partners are willing to see things from each other's perspective, happiness is not a difficult thing.
Many people, after arriving abroad, go through a period of not fitting in — this is the so-called "culture shock."
At first everything feels fresh: the streets, the food, the language — even the way people talk is different from back home.
But after a few weeks, the feeling of novelty slowly fades, and all kinds of difficulties appear.
For example, you may not understand the local people's jokes, nor know how to communicate with them.
Some people therefore feel lonely, and even regret leaving their own country.
Psychologists believe this is a normal stage that almost every overseas student has been through.
If you want to adapt faster, the best way is to take the initiative to make friends and join more local activities.
As time goes on, you will find that both cultures can bring you joy.
So when you meet culture shock, don't be afraid — it is actually a part of growing up.
China's territory is vast and its dialects are numerous — from Cantonese to Shanghainese, almost every place has its own unique accent.
However, as Mandarin education has spread, more and more children speak only Mandarin from a young age, and dialects are gradually disappearing.
Some worry that once a dialect disappears, the local culture and historical memory associated with it will disappear along with it.
My cousin grew up in Guangzhou; she says only when she speaks Cantonese does she truly feel she has "returned home."
To her, dialect is not only a tool for communication, but even more a symbol of identity.
On the contrary, some believe that promoting Mandarin helps people from different regions communicate smoothly, thereby promoting social integration.
In recent years, some cities have begun offering dialect courses in schools, hoping that through education the younger generation will rediscover their own "hometown accent."
In the final analysis, dialects and Mandarin are not an either-or choice; the two can completely coexist in daily life.
With the development of the times, many traditional crafts are slowly disappearing.
My grandfather is a carpenter; the furniture he makes uses not a single nail, yet it is sturdy enough to last for decades.
In the past, almost every old street had a blacksmith, a tailor, and a shoe-repair master.
Nowadays factory-made goods are both cheap and convenient, and fewer and fewer young people are willing to learn a craft.
A craft often takes more than a decade of practice, yet the income is not high; this is the main reason it is disappearing.
Grandpa often says, "Machines work fast, but they cannot produce the warmth of human hands."
Fortunately, some people have begun recording these old crafts online, attracting quite a few viewers.
After watching, some young people make special trips to the countryside to learn from the old masters.
Traditional crafts are not only a kind of skill, but also the living memory of generation after generation.
In China, the intensity of educational competition often astonishes my foreign friends.
Many children start attending all kinds of extra classes as early as kindergarten.
The reason parents are so anxious is that they believe education is the only chance to change one's fate.
One mother once told me: "I know my child is exhausted, but everyone else is studying, so we don't dare to stop."
This phenomenon has a vivid name: "neijuan", or involution.
On the one hand, competition pushes children to study hard; on the other hand, excessive pressure harms their physical and mental health.
In recent years, the government has introduced policies to lighten students' burden.
Rather than making children study in such misery, it would be better to help them keep their interest in learning.
After all, life is a marathon, not a sprint.
Ten years ago, you could hardly see any new energy vehicles on the streets of China.
Today the situation is completely different: green-plated electric cars are everywhere on the roads.
The reason they have developed so quickly is that the government strongly supports them and the technology keeps maturing.
On the one hand, electric cars do not pollute the air, which is a great benefit for the environment; on the other hand, they also cost less to run than traditional cars.
Of course, there are still plenty of problems: charging is not very convenient, and battery performance in winter is a real worry.
A friend of mine bought an electric car last year, and he says he never wants to go back to the days of filling up with gas.
But he also admits that before every long trip, he has no choice but to plan out the charging stops in advance.
As charging stations become more and more widespread, these problems will gradually be solved.
In my view, new energy vehicles represent the trend of the future, and this change has only just begun.
Three years ago, I used 20,000 yuan of my own savings to open a small milk tea shop.
On opening day, I was especially excited, thinking I would soon start making money.
But reality wasn't as simple as I had imagined: rent, ingredients, employee wages — every item cost money.
In the first month, I barely rested at all, working over ten hours every day.
What worried me even more was that two other milk tea shops selling the same thing opened nearby, and competition suddenly became fierce.
Half a year later, business at the shop kept getting worse, and I had no choice but to close it.
During that period, I felt like I had failed, and I was even a bit embarrassed to tell my friends about it.
But looking back now, that startup experience taught me a lot: managing money, reading the market, dealing with people.
I often tell myself: failing at your first startup isn't scary; what's scary is being too afraid of failure to try again.
Last weekend I watched a food documentary, and there was one shot in it that left me especially unforgettable.
In the shot, a grandmother in Yunnan gets up at four in the morning and grinds rice alone in the kitchen.
She said she has been grinding rice like this for more than forty years and has never once stopped.
The ground rice needs to ferment overnight; only at noon the next day can it be made into a bowl of steaming-hot rice noodles.
The director did not interview any master chefs, and there was no competition — the camera only showed ordinary people cooking.
But I was deeply moved, because behind every simple movement was decades of persistence.
A good food documentary is actually filming not just the dishes, but the people who cook and their lives.
After I finished watching, I called my mom and asked what she thinks about while cooking.
She said with a smile: "I just want you all to eat happily — that's enough."
In the center of Beijing stands the largest palace complex in the world: the Forbidden City.
Construction of the Forbidden City began in 1406 and was completed in 1420, taking fourteen years in all.
From the Ming dynasty to the Qing dynasty, twenty-four emperors in succession lived here and handled the affairs of state.
Legend says the Forbidden City has nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine and a half rooms; the actual number is not that high, but it is still enough to amaze people.
