Most of the roofs of the Forbidden City are yellow, because in ancient times yellow was a color that only the emperor could use.
In 1925, the Forbidden City became a museum, and ordinary people could walk into the emperor's home for the first time.
When it snows in winter, the red walls, white snow, and golden roofs come together, as beautiful as a painting.
Today, over ten million visitors come here every year to experience six hundred years of history.
From the emperor's home to the people's museum, the transformation of this palace is itself a moving story.
The paper you use every day and the map in your phone are actually connected to Chinese inventions from more than a thousand years ago.
China's Four Great Inventions of ancient times are made up of papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and the compass.
Before paper was invented, people wrote characters on bamboo, and a single book was so heavy that a cart was needed to pull it.
Cai Lun of the Han dynasty improved papermaking, and from then on ordinary people could also afford to read books.
After printing appeared, books became cheaper and cheaper, and knowledge quickly spread into the hands of more people.
Gunpowder was discovered by chance while people were searching for medicine, yet later it turned into the beautiful fireworks of festivals.
The compass helped ships find their direction on the sea; every ship that sailed far away could not do without it.
The map in today's mobile phone is really the compass's "grandson".
A sheet of paper, a book, a trip — they all remind us that great inventions often come from small problems in daily life.
The "generation gap" refers to the differences between two generations in their ways of thinking and ways of life.
The parents' generation lives frugally and likes to save money, yet young people are willing to spend money to enjoy life.
When it comes to finding a job, parents hope their children will find stable work, yet the children value interest and freedom more.
Dating and marriage are also a common source of conflict: many parents are anxious, yet young people feel there is no need to marry too early.
Some children feel their parents don't understand them, and gradually become unwilling to share their true feelings with them.
Actually, it is quite normal for a generation gap to arise, because the two generations grew up in different times.
To reduce the generation gap, the key lies in communication: parents should listen carefully to their children's ideas, and children should have a bit more patience.
As long as both sides respect each other, the two generations can surely become good friends.
Going home for Spring Festival, I almost failed to recognize my own hometown.
When I was little, in front of our house was a dirt road, and whenever it rained there was mud everywhere.
Now it has become a wide paved road, and at night the streetlights make it as bright as day.
In the past, the young people of the village all went to big cities to work, leaving only the elderly and children behind.
In recent years quite a few people have come back; some run online shops selling hometown apples, and business is incredibly good.
My cousin is one of them; he says, "Rather than working for someone else in a big city, it's better to come home and build a career of your own."
Of course, there are changes that make me sad too: the primary school I attended has closed, because there are fewer and fewer children.
The old tree at the village entrance is still there, but the old folks playing chess under it are a different group now.
My hometown has become more convenient and more beautiful, but some things, once lost, can never be found again.
The first time I used WeChat was in 2012, when it was still just an app for sending messages.
Now when I open my phone, almost everything I do in a day gets done inside this one app.
In the morning I buy groceries with it, at noon I pay with it, and in the evening I call my parents back home with it.
My mother is over sixty; she used to not even know how to send a text, yet nowadays she sends more voice messages in the family group than anybody.
It is genuinely convenient, of course, but the trouble came along with it.
A message your boss sends late at night cannot go unanswered, yet answering it amounts to agreeing to work overtime.
Someone joked that WeChat has made work hours and off hours impossible to tell apart.
In my view the tool itself is not at fault; what is wrong is that we have turned it into the whole of life.
So over the past two years I have done one small thing: after ten at night, I turn off notifications from the work groups.
The messages are still there the next day, but my evenings have finally become mine again.
I have a friend who, for the past six months, has been reading the same kind of news online every single day.
He opens his phone, and the content recommended to him always matches the way he already thinks.
After a while, he came to feel that everyone in the world thinks exactly the way he does.
This situation has a name: the information cocoon. Layer by layer, we wrap ourselves up in the information we like.
The interesting part is that we are not necessarily shut in by other people; it is precisely we ourselves who chose it.
Every time we watch one more video, the machine records it once; over time, it shows us only the things we love to watch.
Rather than blaming the app, we might as well ask ourselves: when was the last time we carefully read an article we disagreed with?
I tried a method: every week I deliberately follow three writers whose views are the opposite of mine.
Honestly, it feels unpleasant while I read; but after the discomfort, I find that my own thinking has actually become clearer.
Have you ever heard of "intangible cultural heritage"?
It refers to culture that cannot be seen or touched, yet has been passed down generation after generation, such as paper cutting, shadow puppetry, and traditional festivals.
In 2001, China's Kunqu opera was placed by the United Nations on the world intangible cultural heritage list.
Later, the Dragon Boat Festival, Peking opera, and Chinese acupuncture also became world-level cultural heritage one after another.
The reason these cultures must be protected is that once they disappear, they can never be recovered.
In a small town in the south, I once watched an old man perform shadow puppetry.
Under the lamplight, with just a pair of hands he made the shadows sing and dance on a white cloth, and the audience watched, entranced.
Now, many schools invite folk performers to give lessons, letting children come into contact with these traditions from a young age.
Protecting heritage does not mean putting it into a museum, but rather letting it continue to live in people's daily lives.
If you want to understand young people in China today, there are two words you must know: neijuan (involution) and tangping (lying flat).
"Involution" refers to a kind of meaningless competition: everyone works harder and harder, yet what they get does not increase.
For example, in some companies one person volunteers to work overtime, so everyone else has no choice but to follow; in the end everyone is more exhausted, yet salaries haven't risen a cent.
"Lying flat" is the answer to involution: since hard work is useless, I will lower my desires — no buying a house, no getting married, just doing the most basic work.
My cousin is exactly like this. He says: "Rather than keep competing in a big city, I'd rather go back to my hometown and live a quiet life."
Their parents' generation criticizes this attitude as too negative, but young people feel it is not laziness — it is a kind of clear-headedness.
The interesting thing is, many people who say they are going to lie flat still show up to work on time the next day.
Perhaps lying flat is more like a mood — a way of protecting oneself under pressure.
Those who completely lie flat are a minority; most people are somewhere between involution and lying flat, searching for a position they can accept.
At six in the morning, before the sky is fully light, the Lanzhou noodle shop downstairs from my home is already open.
The owner is from Gansu; he came to this city twenty years ago and raised two children with his own two hands.
I often sit by the window and watch him pull the noodles: a lump of dough stretches long and thin in his hands, turning into fine noodles in just a few seconds.
The noodles go into the pot, the aroma of beef soup slowly drifts out, and the whole little shop fills with steam.
A proper bowl of Lanzhou noodles follows the rule of "one clear, two white, three red, four green": clear soup, white radish, red chili, green cilantro.
The owner says the soup starts simmering at three in the morning; the beef bones must be boiled for more than five hours.
Most customers are people rushing to work: they finish a bowl in ten minutes, heads covered in sweat, then walk out into the cold wind.
Someone once asked the owner why he doesn't open a few more shops and earn a bit more money.
He smiled and shook his head: "Open too many shops, and the soup won't taste like this anymore."
Behind every bowl of good noodles, there are decades of one person's patience.
In China, there is almost no one who does not know the name Li Bai.
He was one of the most famous poets of the Tang dynasty, and people call him the "Immortal Poet".
In his lifetime, Li Bai wrote about one thousand poems, many of which are related to the moon.
One quiet night, watching the moonlight before his bed, he thought of his faraway home.
So he wrote the famous "Quiet Night Thoughts": "Raising my head, I gaze at the bright moon; lowering my head, I think of my hometown."
In just ten characters, it captures with perfect clarity the feeling of missing home while far away.
Legend says Li Bai especially loved wine; after drinking, he would often raise his cup to the moon and treat it as his own friend.
Some even say that in the end, it was while trying to grab hold of the moon in the water that he fell into a river.
More than a thousand years have passed, yet whenever people raise their heads and see the moon, they still think of this poet who loved it.
When I moved house last year, I counted and found I somehow owned more than two hundred pieces of clothing — many still with the tags on.
In that moment, I decided to try the "minimalist living" my friend often talked about.
Minimalism is not buying nothing at all; it is keeping only the things you truly need and truly love.
I used a simple standard: anything I hadn't used in a year could basically be given away or thrown out.
The sorting process was painful; several times I stood holding an old sweater thinking: what if I need it someday?
The facts proved that this "someday" almost never came.
Now my room is half empty: finding things is faster, cleaning is easier, and even the time spent choosing clothes in the morning has gotten shorter.
Even more unexpectedly, once I owned less, I became more careful about buying: before every purchase, I ask myself three times.
For me, minimalism is not the goal itself, but a method for letting life return to what matters.
A few years ago, Princeton University conducted a famous study investigating the relationship between money and happiness.
The research found that the higher the income, the happier people indeed are, but this relationship only holds up to a certain number.
After annual income reaches around seventy-five thousand dollars, additional money has less and less influence on happiness.
In other words, money can keep people from worrying about rent, medical bills, and meals — and that's already the greater part of happiness.
But beyond that line, happiness comes more from friends, family, and meaningful things, rather than the number on a bank card.
I know an engineer whose salary is very high, yet he often works overtime until late at night and almost has no time to see friends.
He said of himself: "the richer I get, the lonelier I feel" — those words left a deep impression on me.
Later he switched to a job with a lower salary but that let him leave work on time; he said he was, on the contrary, much happier.
This research reminds us: money is important, but past a certain point, happiness depends on other things.
Last month, my friend Xiaoyu posted a selfie online; unexpectedly, she received a lot of unpleasant comments.
Some people insulted her looks, calling her ugly, and others said she simply shouldn't appear online at all.
Within a single day, more and more people were insulting her, and Xiaoyu was so scared that she no longer dared to open her phone.
This kind of behavior — hiding behind a screen to attack others — is exactly what we commonly call "online violence" (cyberbullying).
What's strange is that most of the people insulting her didn't know Xiaoyu at all.
Perhaps because they can't see the other person's expression, many people actually find it easier to lose their sense of restraint when speaking.
Xiaoyu's mood grew worse and worse; she even began to wonder whether she had really done something wrong.
Later, her older brother urged her to take screenshots of those comments and save them, then report them to the platform.
Slowly, Xiaoyu came to understand: no matter how loud the online insults are, they don't represent the true thoughts of most people.
With the development of the internet, online shopping has become more and more common.
Without leaving home, people can buy products from all over the world.
Although online shopping is convenient, it also has some problems.
For example, some products are of poor quality and look completely different from the pictures.
Therefore, consumers should stay calm when shopping and avoid spending blindly.
Starting in the 1980s, China implemented the one-child policy.
As a result, an entire generation grew up without any brothers or sisters.
Many people assume that only children, doted on by their parents from an early age, must be selfish.
In fact, this notion is not fair at all.
Many of the only children I know are, on the contrary, remarkably independent and very good at looking after others.
However, they do face enormous pressure: one couple often has to look after four elderly parents.
No matter how capable you are, it is hard to care for the elderly and the children at the same time while still doing your own job well.
As the aging of society grows more serious, this problem is becoming even more pronounced.
The policy has since changed, but the experience of the only-child generation still deeply shapes Chinese ideas about family.
Foreign friends watching Peking opera for the first time are often captivated by the colors on the actors' faces.
This kind of "makeup" painted on the face has a special name: lianpu, the painted mask.
The colors of the masks are not chosen casually; each color represents a type of personality.
Red represents loyalty and bravery; the most famous red face is the ancient hero Guan Yu.
Black represents justice: Lord Bao, the most just figure in legend, has a black face.
White is just the opposite: it represents dishonesty, and Cao Cao of the Three Kingdoms is often painted with a white face.
So as soon as experienced audience members see the mask, they know who is good and who is bad, without hearing a single word.
Nowadays, the painted masks have long since stepped down from the stage, appearing on clothes, cups, and stamps.
No matter whether you understand Chinese or not, you can read wonderful stories out of these colors.
My friend Xiaoyu has no children, but she keeps a cat — the money she spends on the cat each month is even more than what she spends on herself for food.
The cat food has to be imported, the toys get replaced every month, and even the cat litter has to be an imported brand.
Last month the cat caught a cold, and just one visit to the pet hospital cost more than two thousand yuan.
Xiaoyu said: "When a person gets sick and goes to the hospital, it doesn't necessarily cost this much money, but when the cat gets sick, I can't cut corners."
There are more and more people like Xiaoyu, and in recent years the term "pet economy" has also become more and more common.
Data shows that China has more than one hundred million pet cats and dogs, and the related market can reach hundreds of billions of yuan a year.
From pet food and pet hospitals to pet photography and pet insurance, almost every industry is serving pets.
Some people feel it's a waste of money, but to Xiaoyu, the cat has long been family — not as simple as just being a pet.
She said: "It can't talk, but it keeps me company — no amount of money can buy this kind of companionship."
Nowadays, many stores let you pay using face-scan payment, and it takes only a few seconds to complete the payment.
The first time I used it, I found it especially convenient, even a bit exciting.
But after I got home, it suddenly occurred to me: my face had just been stored in someone else's computer, like that.
Phone apps are the same way: as soon as you open one, it seems to already know all my secrets.
I had just chatted with a friend yesterday about wanting to buy running shoes, and today ads for running shoes appeared on my phone.
This makes me both happy and afraid: happy because shopping has become convenient, afraid because I seem to have no secrets left.
Experts say convenience and privacy are like the two ends of a scale: when one side gets heavier, the other side gets lighter.
While we enjoy the convenience brought by technology, we should also ask ourselves: how much privacy are we willing to give up for it?
Perhaps there's no right or wrong answer, but at least we should clearly know what kind of choice we are making.
After the epidemic, our company allowed employees to work from home three days a week.
At first, I thought it was the happiest thing in the world: no squeezing onto the subway, no formal clothes, and I could even pet the cat during meetings.
But three months later, I discovered things were not that simple.
At home, the boundary between work and life became more and more blurry.
At ten in the evening, colleagues are still sending messages in the group chat — do you reply or not?
I also began to miss the boring little things at the office: lunch with colleagues at noon, someone treating everyone to coffee in the afternoon.
It turns out what I missed was not the office, but the warmth between people.
Now I go to the company two days a week and work from home three days, and I have slowly found a balance.
Remote work is not that good, nor that bad — it is simply a new way of living that we have to learn to manage ourselves.
In China's big cities there is a special kind of home, known as "school-district housing".
The house itself may be small and old, yet the price is shockingly high.
The reason is simple: buy it, and your child can enter the best school in the area.
For their children's education, many parents have no choice but to spend all their savings, or even borrow heavily.
One of my colleagues did exactly that: he sold his spacious house and moved into a fifty-square-meter old apartment.
He said with a smile: "The place is a bit old, sure, but my child's future can't wait."
The school-district housing phenomenon reflects the uneven distribution of educational resources.
Wherever good schools are concentrated, housing prices are invariably sky-high.
In recent years the government has been looking for ways to make educational resources fairer, but solving the problem completely will, I'm afraid, take a very long time.
Ten years ago, shared bikes, shared power banks, and shared umbrellas appeared almost overnight in the streets and alleys of China.
At the time, almost everyone believed that "anything can be shared" would completely transform people's way of life.
However, once the craze passed, many sharing-economy companies, unable to turn a profit, went bankrupt one after another.
Take shared bikes as an example: because vehicle damage was severe and maintenance costs too high, quite a few companies ultimately had no choice but to declare bankruptcy.
Besides this, the uneven conduct of users was also a problem that could not be ignored: some people deliberately damaged bikes, even hiding them away for private use.
By contrast, shared power banks actually survived, because they met people's genuine need for emergency charging while out and about.
This shows that whether a sharing-economy project can survive long term hinges on whether it truly solves a real problem for users.
Today, abandoned shared bikes piled up like mountains on the streets have become the most visible mark left behind by this ebb tide.
Last week, I saw on my social media feed that my college classmate Xiaolin had gotten married, and I immediately sent her a message.
We arranged to meet up on the weekend, and I was really looking forward to it — after all, we hadn't seen each other in five years.
The day we met, we chatted for two hours, but no matter what we talked about, it all seemed to be just polite small talk.
We used to be able to talk about anything, but now it seemed like we couldn't find common topics anymore.
After we parted, I felt a bit down inside, and couldn't help wondering: does friendship have a shelf life too?
Later I slowly came to understand: it's not that our feelings had faded, but that our lives had headed in different directions.
She is busy taking care of her child every day, while I'm busy working overtime every day, so naturally the things we care about are different.
Maybe friendship doesn't need to stay lively all the time; as long as we can still think of each other when needed, that's already precious.
I decided not to feel sad about this kind of change anymore, and instead to cherish the friends around me now.
Before going to sleep at night, I tell myself: only ten minutes of short videos.
By the time I look at the clock again, it is already one in the morning.
I believe many people have had the same experience as me.
Short videos have indeed given us a lot: learn a dish in three minutes, catch up on a news story in one minute, and countless moments that make us laugh out loud.
But they have also quietly changed us: I find it harder and harder to finish a book, and even a two-hour movie feels too long.
Our patience seems to have been swiped away, one second at a time.
Some people say we should delete these apps; I have tried three times, and failed every time.
Later I switched to another method: not quitting completely, but setting a rule to watch only half an hour after dinner.
Even if I only manage half of it, it is still better than lying in bed scrolling until midnight.
Tools are neither good nor bad; the key question is: in the end, are we using them, or are they using us?
Many people assume Sichuan cuisine is simply "spicy," but actually its most impressive quality is the layering of its flavors.
Last month I learned to cook from a Sichuan cuisine chef, and his very first sentence was: "Sichuan food isn't just spicy — there are more than twenty flavors."
He first made a dish of fish-fragrant shredded pork; strangely, this dish had no fish in it at all, yet had a faint fish-fragrant taste.
The chef said this "fish-fragrance" comes from a combination of pickled chili, ginger, garlic, and sweet-and-sour seasoning — not from actually adding fish.
Next he made a dish of strange-flavor chicken — sour, sweet, numbing, spicy, and salty, all five flavors appearing on the tongue at once.
There's also a preparation called "lychee flavor" — the dish has not a single lychee in it, yet carries a fruit-like sweet fragrance.
The chef said with a smile: "The philosophy of Sichuan cuisine is telling a story with different flavors — spiciness is just the beginning, not the end."
After that day I finally understood: people who truly understand Sichuan cuisine are eating not for the spice, but for the layers.
Over two thousand years ago, in the Han dynasty, an envoy named Zhang Qian set out from Chang'an and headed all the way west.
His journey was extremely hard, but it opened up a passage connecting China with the West.
Because Chinese silk was the most famous thing on this road, later generations called it the "Silk Road."
Merchants drove camels, transporting silk, tea, and porcelain to the West.
At the same time, grapes, fine Western horses, and other things were introduced into China.
What was exchanged along this road was not only goods, but also ideas, music, and technology.
Buddhism, in fact, spread from India to China along this very road.
Imagine it: in the desert night, a camel caravan advances slowly under the starry sky, walking for months at a stretch.
One road allowed different civilizations to meet, and it changed the history of the world.
Last month I kept having trouble sleeping, so a friend suggested I try some "sleep aid" products.
I first bought a bottle of melatonin, then a white-noise machine, spending over three hundred yuan in total.
Later I learned that all of these belong to the "sleep economy" — a market that has emerged specifically to help people sleep well.
It's said that in just last year alone, the size of this market exceeded 400 billion yuan.
Besides melatonin and white-noise machines, there are also smart wristbands specifically designed to track people's sleep time.
To be honest, after buying these things, I really did sleep a little better.
But one night, I suddenly noticed myself lying in bed, wearing the wristband on one hand while still scrolling on my phone.
At that moment I finally understood: what was really keeping me awake probably wasn't a lack of tools, but my reluctance to put down my phone.
Since then, I've started putting my phone in another room before bed, and the effect has been better than any product.
Every year around Spring Festival, China sees what can be called the largest-scale population migration in the world — this is the so-called "chunyun."
During this period, hundreds of millions of people rush back from the cities where they work to their hometowns, just to eat a reunion dinner with family.
Because train tickets are scarce, many people have no choice but to sit up at their computers in the middle of the night, refreshing the page over and over to grab a ticket.
When my father was young, he once stood for a full twenty-some hours on a train, before finally getting from Guangzhou back to his hometown in Sichuan.
As the high-speed rail network has kept expanding, the journey home has become much faster, but the pressure of grabbing tickets has not eased in the slightest.
At the same time, some people choose not to return to their hometown at all, but instead bring their parents to the city where they work to celebrate the New Year together.
In their view, the location of the reunion isn't important — what matters is whether family can gather together.
Chunyun is not only a test of the transportation system — even more, it reflects Chinese people's unchanging feelings toward the word "home."
Nowadays, studying abroad is nothing new — every year hundreds of thousands of students go overseas to study.
The benefits of studying abroad are obvious: you can improve your foreign language, learn about different cultures, and train your ability to live independently.
Alone in a foreign country, you have to handle everything yourself, which makes many overseas students become more mature.
But studying abroad also has a side of loss.
First, studying abroad is very expensive and may use up money that parents have saved over many years.
Second, overseas students are far from their families and often feel especially homesick during the holidays.
In addition, after graduating, some people neither understand the situation back home nor can fully enter the foreign society, feeling that they stand between two cultures.
Therefore, whether or not to study abroad should be decided according to your own situation, not just by watching what others do.
Last month I went back to my hometown and gave my mom three smartphone lessons.
The first lesson taught her video calls, the second taught her to pay by phone, and the third taught her how to close those cheating ads.
To be honest, in the first two lessons I explained things too fast, and inside I did not have much patience either.
She could not remember the steps and asked the same question four or five times; the moment my tone turned hard, she no longer dared to ask.
That evening I saw that she had written every single step into a little notebook, in big characters, very carefully.
I suddenly remembered my childhood: she taught me to write, repeating a single character dozens of times, and never once lost her temper.
The next day I slowed down by half, and she actually learned faster than the day before.
On the day I left, she sent me her first voice message: Son, message me when you get there.
We always say our parents cannot keep up with the times; in fact, all they lack is a teacher willing to slow down.
In recent years there have been more and more marathons at home, and the number of people signing up is often more than ten times the available places.
My first race was three years ago, and when I reached the thirtieth kilometer I seriously thought about quitting.
What kept me going was not determination, but half a bottle of water handed to me by a stranger at the roadside.
Many people who run marathons today are actually not doing it for their finishing time at all.
Some run to lose weight, some to post one photo online, and others just want to get back a little control over their lives.
Some people also criticize all this: cities treat the race as an advertisement, and runners treat their times as a matter of face.
These criticisms are not necessarily unreasonable, but I always feel that things able to make tens of thousands of people willingly get up early to train are rare in themselves.
The truly hard part of a marathon is not those forty-two kilometers, but putting on your shoes and stepping out alone on a morning when nobody is watching.
Once that step is taken, the result of the race no longer seems so important.
A few years ago, what colleagues chatted about was buying a house; these past two years, the topic has become side jobs.
Some drive to earn money after work, some teach cooking on weekends, and others sell photos they took themselves online.
Out loud everyone says it is for interest, but what they are really thinking about is a sense of security.
No matter how stable a job is, it can still vanish in one round of restructuring, and we have seen far too much of that these past few years.
So people say that a side job has gone from being a hobby to being a basic necessity.
Yet among the ten friends I know with side jobs, fewer than three actually make money.
Most of the rest trade their rest time for a little income, while slowly spending away their health and energy.
Rather than rushing to find a side job that pays right away, it is better to think this through first: will this still be worth doing three years from now?
The real meaning of a side job is perhaps not one extra income, but that when life is pushing you along, you still hold another road in your hand.
In recent decades, as Western medicine has spread in China, the status of traditional Chinese medicine has gone through a process of being doubted and then re-valued.
Supporters believe that Chinese medicine emphasizes "regulation" and "holism," and has effects on certain chronic diseases that Western medicine finds hard to replace.
However, opponents point out that many of Chinese medicine's theories lack scientific evidence, and their effects are hard to verify by modern medical standards.
My grandmother drinks herbal medicine year-round to nurse her body; she says Chinese medicine treats the "root cause," while Western medicine treats the "symptoms."
At the same time, more and more young people are starting to try traditional therapies like acupuncture and cupping, treating them as a fashionable form of wellness.
Not only have Chinese people rediscovered their interest in Chinese medicine, many foreigners have also started learning acupuncture and tuina massage.
As a result, the traditional Chinese medicine industry has developed rapidly in recent years, and related health products and clinics can be seen everywhere in cities.
In any case, against the backdrop of combining Chinese and Western medicine, if Chinese medicine truly wants to go global, it still needs a great deal more scientific verification.
In recent decades, more and more people from the countryside have left their hometowns to work and live in big cities.
This phenomenon is called "urbanization," and it is changing our society.
On the one hand, cities can offer more job opportunities and better educational conditions.
In the city, young people find it easier to realize their dreams, and incomes are much higher than in the countryside.
But on the other hand, urbanization has also brought quite a few problems, such as crowded traffic, expensive rent, and environmental pollution.
Meanwhile, only the elderly and children remain in the villages, and much of the land has no one to farm it.
Some people think we should keep developing big cities, while others advocate putting more resources into the countryside.
In my view, both cities and the countryside need to develop; the key is to let people freely choose their own way of life.
As a child, I thought happiness was simply scoring one hundred on a test, so Mom would buy me candy.
After growing up, happiness seemed to turn into a competition: a better job, a bigger house, a more expensive car.
But strangely, the more we obtain, the more anxious we become instead.
Last year I fell ill and stayed in the hospital for two weeks.
Lying in the hospital bed, I suddenly understood: being able to walk on my own, eat a proper meal, sleep a sound night's sleep — it turns out these are all happiness.
The day I left the hospital, the sunshine fell on my face and I almost cried.
Scientists say people quickly get used to the feeling of happiness; this is called "adaptation".
So happiness is not a result, but an ability: the ability to notice the small good things in life.
Rather than envying other people's lives, it is better to earnestly live your own today well.
What is happiness? Perhaps it is hiding in the cup of hot tea you drink today.
Over six hundred years ago, in the Ming dynasty, China had a great navigator named Zheng He.
From 1405 to 1433, he led fleets on seven voyages to the Western Seas, visiting more than thirty countries and regions.
His fleet was enormous in scale: at its largest it had over two hundred ships and more than twenty-seven thousand people.
The largest of these ships were called "treasure ships"; they are said to have been over a hundred meters long, like palaces on the sea.
The fleet carried silk, porcelain, and tea abroad, and also brought back spices and other local specialties from many lands.
Most interestingly, on one voyage the fleet brought back a giraffe, and the whole city ran to see this magical animal.
Nearly everywhere the fleet went, it left behind friendly memories.
After Zheng He passed away, ocean voyages on such a large scale came to an end.
Today people still commemorate him, because he proved that the ocean can link the world together.
Every so often someone declares that the golden age of science fiction is over.
In the fifties and sixties humankind had only just turned its gaze toward space, and writers dared, on the strength of a few pages of sketches, to imagine the fate of an entire galaxy.
The science fiction of that era was full of optimism: technology was seen as a stairway to the future, not as a sword hanging overhead.

By contrast, today's science fiction is often wrapped in shadow: climate collapse, artificial intelligence running loose, surveillance seeping into every crack — these have become an almost fixed backdrop.
And so people sigh that we have lost the ability to dream.
But rather than say that imagination has declined, it is better to say that it has changed direction.
Early science fiction answered the question "what can we build"; contemporary science fiction presses a different one: "once it is built, do we still count as human?"
In that sense the golden age has not ended at all; it has merely turned from infatuation with machines to doubt about ourselves.
An age that can face its costs without flinching is not necessarily inferior to an age that only sings the praises of progress.
Nowadays, music, video, shopping, and even news feeds almost all rely on algorithms to make precise recommendations based on users' past clicks and preferences.
This mechanism has admittedly brought unprecedented convenience, letting people quickly find the things they like amid a vast ocean of information.
However, while catering to existing preferences, algorithms have also quietly compressed the space in which chance exists, making opportunities to brush past unfamiliar fields increasingly rare.
Imagine twenty years ago: if a person casually flipped through a record store and happened upon an album strikingly different in style, this would often spark a brand-new interest.
Such a fortuitous, accidental gain could even completely change a person's later career path, and all of this stemmed from the randomness that the environment itself preserved.

Conversely, under today's recommendation systems, the content users encounter is mostly an extension of their past selves, while the possibility of anything unfamiliar and out of place has long since been filtered out, layer by layer.
In the final analysis, what algorithms optimize for is certainty, whereas people's growth, friendships, and even career choices often depend on chances that cannot be predicted.

Therefore, rather than simply regarding algorithms as a fearsome scourge, it would be better to consciously leave room for chance from the very outset of design, letting people once again have the freedom to get lost.
What is most fascinating about archaeology is that it often overturns our fixed understanding of the past when we least expect it.
Not long ago, an archaeological team unexpectedly unearthed a well-preserved batch of stone tools and pottery shards at a river valley site.
At first, based on the soil strata, researchers judged that these artifacts dated back several thousand years, consistent with the locally known civilization.
However, once the carbon-14 dating results came in, they pushed the date back significantly — several thousand years earlier than originally estimated.
If this result holds up, it would mean that the history of human activity in the region needs to be rewritten.
After the news broke, the academic world was in an uproar — some were excited, while others questioned whether the dating samples had been contaminated.
The professor leading the excavation stressed that any disruptive conclusion must withstand peer review, and that one dating result alone should not lead to a hasty conclusion.
Currently, the team is expanding the excavation area and inviting multiple independent laboratories to re-test the samples, striving to let the evidence speak for itself.
Whatever the final conclusion turns out to be, this discovery reminds us: history is not a fixed, unchanging verdict, but a story that keeps being retold as new evidence emerges.
Translation is far from a simple matter of swapping the words of one language for those of another; it is the art of building a bridge between two cultures.
In the West there is a famous saying — "to translate is to betray" — because no translation can ever be completely faithful to the original.
Take the word yuanfen: English has no ready-made equivalent, so the translator can only spend a whole sentence explaining this connection too wonderful for words.
Likewise, translate English humor literally into Chinese and the joke usually vanishes without a trace; a masterly translator will start from scratch and make readers laugh in Chinese's own way.
The translation world has a three-character standard — xin, da, ya: be faithful to the original meaning, read smoothly and fluently, and preserve the spirit of the original.
The three often conflict with one another, and the translator is forced to make painful trade-offs between faithfulness and beauty.
The reason we call translation an art rather than a technique is that it has no single correct answer: every translation is an act of re-creation.
The moment you try translating your favorite line of poetry from your mother tongue into Chinese, you will immediately taste the translator's joys and hardships.
Western languages pursue precision, yet Chinese often excels at vagueness; this vagueness is by no means a defect but a beauty all its own.
A friend asks what time you will arrive, and you answer "around eight"; the host says "sit wherever you like," and the guest says "I'll just have a little of whatever."
A single "more or less" both gives the other person a rough expectation and leaves yourself some leeway — two birds with one stone, as it were.
Chinese painting values empty space, and the Chinese language likewise values what lies beyond the words: say three-tenths, and leave the other seven-tenths for the listener to work out.
Or take "I'll treat you to dinner some other day": the "some other day" is most likely not a concrete date but a way of expressing goodwill.
If beginners take all these phrases at face value, misunderstandings are inevitable; only by grasping the tacit understanding behind the vagueness have you truly crossed the threshold.
Of course, vagueness has its limits: when signing contracts or negotiating prices, Chinese people will haggle over every ounce, with no vagueness whatsoever.
Does your mother tongue also have expressions that "say one half and hold back the other"? Compare them, and you will see both cultures more clearly.
With high-rises standing like forests and streets streaming with traffic, big cities attract countless dream-chasing young people with their bustle and prosperity.
Behind the prosperity, however, 'big-city disease' is becoming increasingly prominent.
Traffic congestion devours people's time, and soaring housing prices leave young people gasping for breath.
Air pollution and noise disturbance further leave urban residents' quality of life greatly compromised.
Some choose to flee 'Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou' and return to smaller cities with a gentler pace.
Others believe that the opportunities and resources of big cities remain irreplaceable.
In fact, the root of the problem lies not in city size itself, but in the imbalance of resource distribution.
Only by promoting coordinated regional development and making smaller cities equally good places to live and work can people truly have the freedom to choose.
Should a city's value, after all, be measured by its height, or by its residents' sense of happiness?
When biodiversity protection comes up, what people picture first is usually a vividly recognizable animal such as the giant panda or the tiger.
But what actually holds up a whole ecosystem is mostly a cast of unglamorous players: fungi in the soil, shellfish on the riverbed, insects in the grass.
One ecologist likens species to the rivets on an aircraft wing: losing one or two seems to matter little, yet nobody can say which one will be the last.

In the nineties, Yellowstone reintroduced wolves; not only were the deer herds brought under control, but the riverbank vegetation recovered along with them, and the shape of the river channel itself unexpectedly changed.
The example shows that the links between species are far closer than we imagine.
And yet stressing "usefulness" alone is not necessarily the safest line of defense.
If a species were proven to have no economic value whatsoever, would we then be free to let it vanish?
To take human usefulness as the only yardstick is in itself a form of arrogance.
Protecting biodiversity is less a matter of rescuing other lives than of keeping in reserve, for ourselves, a road of retreat we have not yet had to walk.
On climate change, the advice the public hears most often is to switch off the lights, use fewer plastic bags, and take public transport whenever possible.
These reminders are of course not wrong, but pushing the whole responsibility onto individuals is a bit too glib.
Studies point out that the emissions an ordinary household saves in a year often fail to offset the consumption of a single large-scale event.
In other words, what really sets the direction of the emissions curve are systemic choices: the energy mix, building standards, transport planning.
Yet if one concludes from this that individuals are powerless, that is equally a misunderstanding.
The reason individual choices matter lies not in how much they directly cut emissions, but in what they shape into being seen as normal.
Only when more and more people take saving energy as a matter of course can policy and the market possibly adjust along with them.
Rather than argue endlessly over "whose fault it is," it would be better to admit that climate responsibility was never a single-choice question.
It needs institutions to turn around and it needs the daily persistence of countless people; the two are equally indispensable.
We like to assume our judgments are objective and rational, yet psychological research shows the human brain comes equipped with all sorts of "cognitive biases."
A cognitive bias is a systematic deviation that occurs when the mind processes information.
Here is a common example: after buying a car of a certain brand, you suddenly notice the same model everywhere on the street.
It is not that there are suddenly more of those cars; rather, your attention is being pulled by "confirmation bias," so you only see evidence that supports your own choice.
Another example: people tend to overestimate their own ability, and paradoxically, the more ignorant a person is, the more confident they tend to be — the so-called "Dunning-Kruger effect."
The reason cognitive biases are so hard to overcome is that they operate outside our awareness; we cannot perceive that we are being swayed by them.

The good news is that although biases can never be fully eliminated, they can be weakened through practice: ask yourself one more question — "Could I be wrong?" — and actively look for evidence against your view.
Admitting that you can be wrong is nothing to be ashamed of; what is truly dangerous is knowing nothing about your own blind spots.
In traditional Chinese culture, collective interests are often placed above individual interests.
As the saying goes, 'the flame leaps high when everyone gathers firewood' — unity and cooperation can indeed create achievements no individual could ever reach.
However, overemphasizing the collective inevitably suppresses individuality, preventing personal creativity from being fully brought into play.
Conversely, Western societies uphold individualism, yet as a result face the predicament of fading human warmth and declining social cohesion.
From this we can see that the collective and the individual are by no means incompatible like fire and water, but rather complement each other.
A healthy society must both safeguard individual freedom and dignity, and cultivate citizens' sense of responsibility.
The key lies in striking the right balance: the collective should not engulf the individual, nor should the individual place itself above the collective.
So when collective and individual interests clash, how exactly should we choose between them?
Bankers understand the power of compound interest: let a small sum keep rolling over, and in a few decades it becomes a considerable fortune.
Habits, in fact, obey the very same law.
Twenty minutes of reading a day adds up to over a hundred hours a year — enough to chew through a dozen thick books.
Conversely, an hour of late-night scrolling every day, accumulated over months and years, overdraws your entire store of energy and health.
The frightening thing about a habit is that its effects are nearly invisible in the short run; good or bad, they only reveal themselves years later.

The British cycling team was once an obscure squad; its new coach pursued no grand reforms, demanding only a one-percent improvement in every detail — and within a few years the team was, astonishingly, sweeping Olympic medals.
Clearly, what determines the course of a life is seldom the grand, dramatic decisions, but the unremarkable little choices made every day.
A habit is a compound-interest account that time opens in our name: whatever you deposit today, you will harvest tomorrow.
Mention Confucianism and many people picture ancient classics and elaborate rituals, seemingly with nothing to do with today's office towers.
Yet whether in teamwork or in relations between boss and subordinate, traces of Confucian thinking can be found everywhere in the modern workplace.
Take "do not impose on others what you do not want for yourself": translated into today's terms, it means don't shove the chores you dislike onto a colleague as if you had every right to.
Or take the idea that "harmony is what matters most": it leads plenty of employees to stay silent in meetings rather than contradict the boss in front of everyone.
Admittedly this keeps the surface calm, yet it can also leave the real problems postponed again and again.
Others argue for dumping the whole tradition and importing a blunt, say-what-you-think style of communication instead.
Rather than simply rejecting it, it is better to keep the "respect" and let go of the "rank by seniority."
One young project manager says that at meetings she always asks the quietest intern to speak first: this preserves the courtesy and forces out the honest words at the same time.
Tradition is not necessarily a constraint; it is more like a language that has to be translated afresh again and again.
In the Tao Te Ching, Laozi wrote: "He who knows contentment is rich."
Read today, more than two thousand years later, these words remain deeply thought-provoking.
Our material conditions far surpass those of the past, yet our sense of happiness has not necessarily grown with them.
Psychologists call this "hedonic adaptation": the thrill of a new car evaporates within three months, and people promptly fix their eyes on the next target.
I know an old carpenter in the countryside who lives in an old house and works with old tools, yet is always beaming; he says: "Enough is enough — craving more only wears you out."
Contentment is not a lack of ambition; it is knowing exactly what is worth chasing and what is merely the burden of vanity.
Desire is like seawater — the more you drink, the thirstier you become; gratitude is like a clear spring — a gentle stream that never runs dry.
Happiness was never on some faraway wish list; it lies in the everyday things we see the moment we lower our heads.
In today's fast-paced society, the term "craftsman spirit" seems somewhat out of step with the times.
And yet it is precisely those craftsmen — patient with solitude, forever striving for perfection — who have created countless breathtaking works.
In Japan there is a sushi master named Jiro Ono; after more than seventy years of making sushi, he is still pondering how to get the temperature of the rice exactly right.
When someone asked him the secret of his success, he said only this: "Do simple things over and over, and do the things you repeat with your whole heart."
The craftsman spirit is by no means stubborn conservatism; it is a pursuit of quality that borders on the ruthless.
At the same time, it is an attitude toward life: refusing to be swayed by restless trends, and focusing on each step of the work at hand.
In an age when everyone chases instant results, slowing down has, paradoxically, become a rare ability.
Craft skills may age, but the craftsman's heart never dies.
The four characters 道法自然 from the Dao De Jing are often rendered as "let nature take its course," but they are in fact far more complicated than that translation suggests.
The "nature" Laozi speaks of is by no means mountains, rivers, grass and trees, but rather the state of things being just as they originally are.
In other words, what it stresses is this: do not use brute force to twist the original rhythm of things.
This shows up clearly in city planning: a river sealed in concrete is actually more likely to flood when a downpour comes.
The "sponge cities" fashionable in recent years let rainwater seep back into the soil, which is to some extent a modern version of that ancient wisdom.
Of course, reading 道法自然 as an excuse to do nothing at all is rather too passive.
The 无为 Laozi talks about means not acting rashly, not refusing to act at all.
A friend who farms told me that the most critical skill in working the land is knowing when to get to work and when to simply wait.
In a life that keeps speeding up, we might as well stop now and then and look at which direction things wanted to grow in the first place.
In an age of information explosion, attention has become one of our scarcest resources.
Many people bustle about all day, only to find that their genuinely important work has barely moved forward.
The reason is simple: their time has been sliced into fragments by email, meetings, and endless notifications.
So-called "deep work" is the ability to concentrate without distraction on a single high-value task for an extended period.
A writer friend of mine has an instructive habit: every morning he locks his phone in a drawer, writes for three hours straight, and only then deals with trivial matters.
As a result, what he finished in one year exceeded the previous three years combined.
Deep work is rare precisely because it goes against the brain's instinct to seek fresh stimulation, and therefore requires deliberate training.
Once you have tasted the rewards of total absorption, it becomes hard to tolerate shallow, fragmented busyness again.
Rather than complaining that there is never enough time, ask yourself: did you set aside one whole, uninterrupted block of time today?
For the past several decades, globalization was regarded as an irreversible tide of history.
Goods, capital, and talent flowed freely across borders, as if the world had become a 'global village.'
In recent years, however, trade protectionism has reared its head, and quite a few countries have built tariff barriers one after another.
The shock of the pandemic further made countries realize that over-reliance on global supply chains harbors enormous risks.
Some people therefore assert that globalization has reached its end.
In my view, this claim is rather an exaggeration.
What is receding is only the old model; in the face of shared challenges such as climate change, the necessity of cooperation is only increasing.
Globalization will not die out; rather, it is seeking a new balance amid twists and turns.
Facing the receding tide, do we choose to build walls, or to build bridges?
In the 1960s, psychologists at Stanford University conducted the famous "marshmallow experiment."
The researchers gave each child a marshmallow and told them: if you can hold out for fifteen minutes without eating it, you will get a second one.
Some children stuffed the candy into their mouths at once; others shut their eyes or sang to distract themselves, and by sheer willpower endured the long wait.
Decades of follow-up showed that the children who could delay gratification generally went on to do better in both school and career.
Delaying gratification is not repressing desire; it is knowing clearly that some rewards are worth trading patience for.
Regrettably, modern life tempts us at every turn to "enjoy it now": takeout arrives in half an hour, short videos switch every three seconds, and even knowledge is sold as "mastered in ten minutes."
The more easily a pleasure is gained, the more quickly it vanishes; the longer a fruit must be waited for, the sweeter it tastes.
Life is like brewing wine: no fierce flame can force out the mellow aroma — only time can bring the flavor to perfection.
Trust in traditional currency is built on national credit: people believe the central bank won't print money arbitrarily, and banks won't abscond with their funds.
Digital currencies, especially cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, propose a completely different model of trust: relying on no institution at all, only on mathematics and code.

Every transaction is recorded on the blockchain and jointly verified by nodes scattered across the globe; tampering with any single record would require simultaneously breaching the vast majority of nodes, which is almost impossible.
In other words, the object of trust shifts from 'some authoritative institution' to 'a set of open, transparent algorithmic rules that anyone can check.'
This design does solve technical problems like double-spending, but it has not solved the problem of drastic price fluctuations.
The price of a single Bitcoin can surge or crash overnight, which makes it feel more like a speculative asset than a stable means of payment.
As a result, the industry has developed 'stablecoins,' which try to peg digital currency to fiat currencies like the US dollar, balancing decentralization with price stability.

In the final analysis, the true value of digital currency lies not in whether it can make you rich overnight, but in the fact that it offers a workable technical solution for transactions that require no trust in a third party.
The moment 'the Mean' is mentioned, many people think of mediocrity, slickness, even spineless fence-sitting.
This is truly a misunderstanding that has lasted two thousand years.
The Mean that Confucius spoke of centers on 'excess is as bad as deficiency': overdoing a thing and underdoing it are equally harmful.
The Mean is by no means the absence of a stance; it is finding, between two extremes, the fulcrum that is exactly right.
It is like simmering a pot of soup: too fierce a flame boils it dry, too low a flame leaves it raw — what a good chef cares about is the control of heat.
In modern life this sense of proportion is everywhere: work hard, but not to the point of overdrawing your health; be sincere with people, but you need not be brutally blunt in every sentence.
In the internet age, black-or-white debates prevail and people rush to pick a side; the middle ground, paradoxically, has become the loneliest place to stand.
Yet truth seldom lives in the loudspeakers at either end; it lives in the quiet middle.
The Mean is not lacking the courage to go to extremes; it is having the power to go to extremes and choosing restraint — and that is what makes it so refined.
Every language has euphemisms, but the Chinese tradition of speaking indirectly runs especially deep: some things cannot be said straight out and must take a detour.

The most typical cases involve age and death: saying someone is "getting on in years" is far more tactful than calling him "old," while "passed away" and "has gone" stand in for that unbearably heavy word "die."

In daily life, someone heading to the restroom will say "I'll just go take care of something convenient," and to talk someone out of a plan, people often say "I'm afraid that might not be quite appropriate."
Workplace indirectness is an art in itself: when the boss says "think it over a bit more," it most likely means he does not approve of your proposal.
The reason euphemism is so highly developed is that Chinese culture places enormous weight on face: a point-blank refusal leaves both sides with no way to climb down gracefully.
So when Chinese people refuse someone, they rarely say "no"; instead they say "I'll do my best" or "let's see when the time comes," and the listener naturally reads between the lines.
For learners, understanding euphemisms is admittedly important, but more important still is learning to use them, so as not to offend anyone without meaning to.
Think about your own language: when you would rather not say "die" or "no" outright, what roundabout expressions do you reach for?
Modern life seems caught in a paradox: transport gets ever faster and communication ever more convenient, yet we always feel short of time.
Speed has admittedly brought efficiency, but it has also cost many people the room to think calmly.
Italy once saw the rise of a "slow food" movement, urging people to sit down and truly savor a meal instead of hastily silencing their stomachs with fast food.
The point of the movement was not to oppose speed itself, but to remind us that the quality of life cannot be measured by speed alone.
Fast and slow are in fact dialectical: drag your feet when speed is needed and you miss opportunities; rush when patience is needed and you plant hidden dangers.
Take learning a skill: the more patiently you work through the basics, the faster you progress later on.
A truly mature person knows how to switch freely between fast and slow, instead of being led by the nose by the pace of the times.
It is worth asking yourself: what in your life deserves to be deliberately slowed down?
On the subway, nearly everyone's head is bowed over a phone, fingertips flying across the screen.
We take in more information every day than in any previous era, yet the knowledge that actually settles in us is pitifully scarce.
The greatest harm of fragmented reading lies in how it robs us of the capacity for deep thought.
A long essay gets squeezed into a three-line summary, a classic gets boiled down to a five-minute video — and just like that, depth of thought is sacrificed.
Neuroscience research shows that a brain long accustomed to skipping and skimming gradually loses the patience to concentrate for extended stretches.

This is not to say fragmented reading is worthless — for picking up information it is admittedly convenient — but letting it replace systematic reading is like living on snacks instead of proper meals.
Reading a thick book is like holding a long conversation: you must slow your pace, weighing and debating with the author again and again.
The more violently the tide of information surges, the more we need a quiet island where we can simply read.
Compress Earth's 4.6-billion-year history into a single day, and the appearance of human civilization takes up less than the final second.
This metaphor is often used to remind people: on a cosmic scale, our existence is how fleeting.
Yet it is precisely within this fleeting instant that humanity developed the ability to alter its own fate — from gene editing to artificial intelligence.
Techno-optimists believe that as long as science keeps advancing, disease, aging, and even resource scarcity will eventually be conquered one by one.
But pessimists remind us that every powerful technology can both benefit humanity and be used toward destruction.
Nuclear energy can both light up the homes of ten thousand families and has once brought devastating disaster — this is the most direct illustration of technology's double-edged nature.
Rather than agonizing over whether humanity will ultimately head toward prosperity or decline, it is better to put our energy into how to set constraints on technology.
Only a civilization capable of restraining itself has earned the right to speak of a long-term future.
After all, what determines whether humanity can carry on has never been technology itself alone, but the wisdom with which we wield it.
In 2018 a Chinese scientist announced the birth of the world's first "gene-edited babies," which immediately drew fierce condemnation worldwide.
The heart of the dispute lies not in the technology itself, but in whether human beings have the standing to rewrite the instruction manual of life.
Supporters point out that if a technology can spare a child the torment of a hereditary disease, refusing to use it is a cruelty of its own.
Opponents, for their part, worry that once the door to editing reproductive cells is opened, the line between "curing" and "enhancing" will grow ever blurrier.
If modifying disease-causing genes is permitted today, will we be choosing height and IQ tomorrow?
An even more practical worry is cost: expensive technology tends to serve the wealthy first, and could thereby carve social inequality into our genes.
It is worth noting that gene therapies used to treat adult patients are far less controversial, because their effects are not passed on to the next generation.
Whether they support it or oppose it, both sides agree on at least one point: a decision like this should not be made by a single laboratory alone.
The faster the technology runs, the more society needs to stop and talk the rules through first.
Ten years ago, when people thought of 'Chinese style' design, what usually came to mind were bright red lanterns and stiff dragon patterns, giving off a stale, dated feel.
Nowadays, things are completely different: young consumers are willing to line up for sneakers, makeup, or even milk tea labeled 'Guochao.'
Behind this trend is homegrown designers' reinterpretation of traditional patterns, calligraphy, and craftsmanship — not merely piling up symbols.
Take a domestic sportswear brand as an example: it combines the colors of Dunhuang murals with the cut of modern sneakers, keeping recognizability without losing a sense of fashion.
An even deeper reason is that this generation's sense of identity with local culture has clearly grown stronger; they no longer feel that 'foreign brands' are the only mark of taste.
At the same time, some companies only bother slapping on a 'Guochao' label while lacking genuine design investment; their products are shoddily made, and consumers quickly see through it.
In other words, whether Guochao can last depends not on whether the pattern is traditional, but on whether the design itself can stand up to aesthetic scrutiny.
True Guochao should be a natural fusion of traditional aesthetics and contemporary lifestyle, not a short-lived marketing show.
Why can some people keep going without any supervision, while others can barely move a step once rewards and punishments are removed?
Psychologists boil the answer down to "intrinsic drive" — that is, motivation that comes from within and needs no external reward.
A classic experiment makes the point well: researchers had two groups of children draw — one group got a prize for each finished drawing, the other got nothing at all.
Weeks later, the children who had been rewarded no longer wanted to draw once the prizes stopped, while the other group still drew with as much delight as ever.
External rewards admittedly work fast, but they quietly corrode a person's interest in the activity itself.
Genuine intrinsic drive usually comes from three elements: room for autonomy, the satisfaction of steadily improving, and a sense that the work is meaningful.
Whether it is learning a language or keeping up a sport, whatever is forced through by sheer willpower mostly ends half-finished, while whatever is driven by interest tends to flow on steadily.
Rather than forcing yourself to work hard, think it through honestly: why, for you, is this thing actually worth doing?
Language is not merely a tool for communication; it is, even more, the vehicle of thought: the language we think in often determines how we see the world.
Linguists once proposed a famous hypothesis: the structure of each language imperceptibly shapes the way its speakers perceive things.
For example, Chinese calls last month "the month above" and next month "the month below," as if time were a river flowing downward, whereas English habitually places the future in front of the body.

Another example: Chinese kinship terms are extremely fine-grained — a maternal uncle, a father's younger brother, and a father's elder brother each have their own word — so speakers must constantly attend to exactly how relatives are related.
This by no means implies that language is a prison locking thought firmly inside; it is more like a pair of glasses that makes certain details exceptionally clear.
People who master a second language often find that when they switch between the two, their personality and tone undergo a subtle change as well.
Learning a foreign language is not so much acquiring new words as acquiring another gaze with which to look at the world.
Next time you speak Chinese, take a moment to notice what this language is quietly steering you to pay attention to, and what it is letting you overlook.
The phrase 'great talent matures late' comes from the Tao Te Ching, meaning that true greatness often needs long years to ripen.
In an era that worships early success, these four characters feel like a dose of good medicine.
The painter Qi Baishi did not settle in Beijing until he was fifty-seven, was still reinventing his style at nearly sixty, and ultimately became the master of his generation.
He was by no means exceptionally gifted; rather, he honed his brushwork day after day for decades, slowly simmering loneliness into mastery.
Look at today, by contrast: many young people, if they have not 'succeeded' by thirty, conclude that they will never amount to anything.
In truth, life is not a sprint but a long marathon, and a slow starter does not necessarily lose at the finish line.
Society's clock is ticking, admittedly, but each of us lives in a time zone of our own.
Some flowers bloom in spring, while others wait until late autumn before bursting into full flower.
Rather than agonize over your age, quietly keep cultivating your craft; a great vessel is finished late precisely because it is so great.
In the era of information explosion, everyone is a receiver of information and, at the same time, a disseminator.
Social media has brought unprecedented convenience, but it has also given rumors wings.
A sensational piece of fake news often spreads faster and wider than a rigorous refutation.
Algorithms push content based on users' preferences, causing people to sink unknowingly into an 'information cocoon.'
Over time, people can only take in voices that match their own position, and social consensus becomes ever harder to form.
Media literacy has therefore become an essential basic ability for modern citizens.
It requires us to verify sources and distinguish truth from falsehood, rather than repost blindly.
Facing the flood of information on our screens, have you ever wondered: are we using the media, or is the media shaping us?
The ancients said: "Dripping water pierces stone."
A single drop of water is insignificant, yet day after day it can pierce through solid stone.
Learning a language is the same: it relies not on momentary enthusiasm, but on long-term accumulation.
Improving a little every day seems tiny, yet it will eventually converge into astonishing change.
So please believe in the power of persistence.
When quantum computing comes up, most people's first reaction is 'a faster computer,' but that understanding is actually not accurate.
Traditional computers store information in 'bits,' where each digit is either 0 or 1; quantum computers instead use 'qubits,' which can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1 simultaneously.
It is precisely this phenomenon of superposition and entanglement that lets quantum computers show potential traditional computers can't hope to match, when handling certain specific problems.

For example, tasks like factoring large numbers or simulating molecular structures could in theory have their computation time shortened by quantum algorithms from tens of thousands of years to just minutes.
However, qubits are extremely susceptible to outside interference; the slightest disturbance can cause 'decoherence,' leading to errors in the computation results.
Therefore, today's most advanced quantum computers still need to operate in environments close to absolute zero, and rely on complex error-correction mechanisms.
What deserves caution is that the media often portrays quantum computing as an 'omnipotent' high technology, while rarely mentioning that it still has a long way to go before practical use.
In other words, quantum computing is not meant to replace traditional computers, but rather to offer a brand-new computational approach for specific fields.
People often assume that memory works like a video camera, preserving experience intact and ready to replay at the press of a button whenever needed.
However, cognitive science research shows that memory is not a one-time recording sealed away forever, but rather a product that the brain reassembles anew each time it recalls.
For example, eyewitnesses to the same car accident often describe the details completely differently, and even the same person's account can subtly change each time it is retold.

What is more unsettling is that the more a memory is retold, the more easily it becomes mixed with the narrator's current emotions and imagination, drifting further and further from the original experience.
Psychologists have induced subjects to "recall" childhood events that never happened, and many people firmly believe these fabricated details, even describing them vividly as if real.
It follows that the vividness of a memory has no necessary connection to its accuracy — a sharp sense of detail may just be an illusion left behind when the brain fills in the gaps.
This finding is especially cautionary for the judicial field: once one relies too heavily on an eyewitness's solemnly sworn testimony, it may result in a wrongful conviction.

Conversely, this also means that the nostalgia and sense of identity we cherish are, to a large extent, built upon memories that are constantly being reshaped, rather than on objective history itself.

In the final analysis, rather than treating memory as a faithful archive, it is better to view it as a story continually revised by one's state of mind — recognizing this is also the beginning of recognizing the limits of the self.
Foreigners newly arrived in China are often puzzled: the work is clearly excellent, yet Chinese people keep saying, "I did it poorly — please give me your guidance."
When praised, replying "oh, not at all" is almost instinctive; people also call their own writing "my clumsy work" and their own views "my shallow opinion."
This modesty is by no means hypocrisy; it is a way of conducting oneself in the world, deeply rooted in the Confucian tradition.
Confucius said, "When three people walk together, one of them is surely my teacher," reminding us that no matter how outstanding we are, we can still learn from others.
In the traditional mindset, flaunting your brilliance not only looks uncultivated but also easily attracts jealousy — as the saying goes, "the gun shoots the bird that sticks its head out."
Playing yourself down a little while talking the other person up thus became a form of etiquette for maintaining interpersonal harmony.
Times are changing, though: in today's job interviews, young people have learned to present their strengths with confidence.
If someone compliments your Chinese, you can either reply modestly, "Oh, I still have a long way to go," or simply smile and say "thank you" — two responses that stand for two different eras.
Think about it: in your culture, what is the best way to accept a compliment?
Two thousand years ago, an old man lived at the frontier; people called him Saiweng, and one day his horse ran off for no reason at all.
His neighbors came one after another to console him, but he said mildly: 'This is not necessarily a bad thing.'
Later, the horse returned leading a fine steed; his son broke his leg riding it; and when war broke out, the lame son was spared from conscription and kept his life.
The textbooks tell us the moral of the story is that 'fortune and misfortune depend on each other.'
But in my view, Saiweng's real gift was not foreseeing the future — it was his refusal to jump to conclusions.
Today we scroll past a piece of news and within seconds rush to like it or rage at it, slapping a label of 'good' or 'bad' on everything.
Yet life is a long film, and we keep trying to judge the entire plot from a single screenshot.
Saiweng's two little words — 'not necessarily' — are a rare kind of mental white space, leaving time itself room to explain.
The next time fate knocks at your door, take a page from the old man: don't applaud just yet — and don't sigh just yet either.
The Little Prince contains a line: "a sense of ritual is precisely what makes one day different from the other days."
This line points to a truth that is easy to overlook: uneventful life needs some markers, or else it blurs into an indistinct mass.
Some people feel that ritual is nothing but a superfluous formality — rather than spending time arranging candles, it's better to save the effort.
But psychological research has found that even a tiny action like lighting a single candle can significantly boost people's sense of satisfaction with the meal that follows.
The reason lies in this: ritual pulls an ordinary matter out of autopilot-like inertia and pulls it back within the scope of our attention.
In other words, the essence of ritual does not lie in how elaborate the form itself is, but in whether it can awaken our awareness of the present moment.
A friend of mine, every time she moves house, stands for one minute at the doorway of her new home and silently bids farewell to her old life.
She says that this one minute, though it changes nothing in reality, truly makes her aware: one chapter has come to an end.
'The great way is utterly simple' comes from Daoist thought: the most fundamental truths of the universe can usually be stated in the plainest words.
Steve Jobs believed this deeply: he pared the phone down to a single button and hid all the complexity out of sight.
Simple, he said, is harder than complex, because you must polish your thinking until it is clear enough.
Our own lives, by contrast, are endless exercises in addition: wardrobes stuffed with clothes, calendars packed with meetings, phones loaded with apps.
We mistakenly assume that the more we own, the closer we are to happiness — and end up so crushed by material craving that we can hardly breathe.
In truth, cutting the complicated down to the simple is a higher-order skill: knowing what you do not want is harder than knowing what you want.
A mountain never explains its height, and the sea never shows off its depth.
True abundance often appears wearing the plainest face.
Only those who have learned to subtract can be said to have truly understood that the great way is simple.
Many people, upon hearing the word 'solitude,' unconsciously equate it with 'loneliness,' as if anyone living alone were doomed to be friendless and melancholy.
However, on closer examination of the two concepts, one finds that solitude is often the result of an active choice, whereas loneliness stems more from a passive, inescapable emotional void.
